Multi-Turn LLM Conversations under the Least-Recently-Used Policy: Mean-Field Asymptotics and Hit Ratio Approximation

Heyuan Yao Affiliation: Northwestern University Affiliation: Evanston, IL 60208 Email: heyuanyao@u.northwestern.edu    Chutong Gao* Affiliation: Purdue University Affiliation: West Lafayette, IN 47907 Email: gao945@purdue.edu    Yuan Lyu* Affiliation: HKUST Affiliation: Hong Kong SAR Email: ylyuad@connect.ust.hk    Izzy Grosof Affiliation: Northwestern University Affiliation: Evanston, IL 60208 Email: izzy.grosof@northwestern.edu    David Simchi-Levi Affiliation: Purdue University Affiliation: West Lafayette, IN 47907 Email: dslevi@purdue.edu
Abstract

The major workloads in modern large language model (LLM) serving systems have shifted from single-shot LLM calls to multi-turn conversations, where new responses are generated based on the whole conversation history across all previous turns. The hit ratio, i.e., the average fraction of KV caches accessed directly from existing caches stored in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), is hence a crucial metric that governs system performance. Estimating the hit ratio is a highly nontrivial task due to the complex system dynamics, where the KV cache prefixes grow with turns and some must be evicted due to finite memory capacity. We formulate the system as a multi-turn conversation model under the least-recently-used (LRU) policy. Through a mean-field asymptotic framework, we prove that as the conversation arrival rate and the memory capacity grow proportionally to infinity, the hit ratio converges to a closed-form limit. Based on the characterization of the limit, we further propose a practical hit ratio estimator, and validate its accuracy by real LLM serving experiments on the Qwen3-8B model implemented on Ascend NPUs. Our results provide a theoretical foundation for the analysis of multi-turn LLM serving systems and a practical guideline for memory capacity provisioning.

*Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Multi-turn interactions have become a core workload form in modern large language model (LLM) services, following the prevalence of coding agents as the most commercially validated LLM application (GitHub (2025); Anthropic (2026)). Within one conversation, coding agents must carry all conversation history (including previous system instructions, history prompt-response pairs, and tool-calling feedback) for new response generation, and such multi-turn LLM calls create prolonged and growing conversation history. A key strategy to hedge against the correspondingly growing compute is context caching, that is, storing and reusing the already generated key-value (KV) caches of the conversation history in the memory or disk, such that new prompts sharing the same history can avoid repeated prefill and thus massively reduce time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inference costs. For example, DeepSeek reports that context caching reduces the TTFT of repetitive 128K-token inputs from 13s to 500ms, and consequently, it charges a prompt that successfully hits the cached content 1/101/10 of the original price (DeepSeek (2024)).

To leverage the maximum value of context caching, it is important to design an LLM serving system that maximizes the long-run average hit ratio, defined as the fraction of KV caches directly reused from the HBM among all KV caches in a generic conversation. A prerequisite for the optimization problem is the following performance analysis problem, which is the focus of this paper:

How to characterize (or approximate) the hit ratio as a function of given system primitives, including the conversation arrival rate, the interarrival-time distribution of prompts within one conversation, the workload distributions, and the offered HBM capacity?

The least-recently-used (LRU) eviction policy.

A conversation history can be reused only if its KV caches remain resident in the HBM memory when a new prompt within the same conversation arrives. However, the HBM memory of the processing unit has only finite capacity and thus inevitably forces eviction of its resident conversations. Throughout the paper we assume the system operates under the LRU eviction policy widely adopted in multi-turn KV-cache management due to its simplicity and empirical success (Wang et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025)). Under LRU, when the amount of KV caches exceeds the HBM capacity, conversations (with its all history KV caches) are evicted sequentially from the least-recently-used one to the most-recently-used one until the capacity constraint is restored.

Overview of our results and contributions.

We make three main contributions.

  • •

    Modeling framework. We propose a parsimonious multi-turn conversation model (MCM) for multi-turn LLM serving under LRU eviction policy, which captures key components that govern the stochastic system dynamics.

  • •

    Mean-field asymptotics. We prove the convergence of the hit ratio to an explicit limit as the conversation arrival rate and the HBM capacity grows proportionally to infinity.

  • •

    Estimator and validation. We derive a theoretically-motivated hit ratio estimator and validate its accuracy in Qwen3-8B model serving experiments implemented on Ascend 910B2 NPUs fed by conversations from the ShareGPT dataset.

2 The Model

In this section, we formulate the MCM under the LRU policy and the corresponding hit ratio. Additional model details, formal policy definitions, and illustrations are provided in Appendix B.

The multi-turn conversation model.

We first introduce the MCM in detail. In LLM practice, KV caches are managed as blocks in the HBM memory, each having a fixed capacity measured in token positions11 1 For instance, in our vLLM-Ascend experiments, each full KV block represents 128 token positions.. We consider a system where the HBM can store at most NN KV blocks, referred to as the HBM capacity. We assume the system is implemented with a Prefill-Decode disaggregation structure with one prefill instance, where the prefill and decode workloads are processed by different machines (prefiller and decoder). The HBM capacity NN under our consideration is that of one prefiller. New conversations arrive according to a Poisson process with rate λ0\lambda_{0}. We assume that the numbers of turns MM of different conversations are i.i.d. Upon arrival of a conversation with its initial prompt tokens, turn-11 starts and the prefiller generates X1X_{1} KV blocks for the prompt. Its corresponding response is immediately generated by one decoder, whose tokens, but not the KV caches22 2 The current Mooncake infrastructure (Qin et al. (2025)) supports the KV block transfer only from a prefiller to a decoder, but not in the reverse direction., are sent back to the prefiller. This marks the end of turn-11. After a random interarrival time WW (i.i.d. across all turns and all conversations), a new prompt of the same conversation arrives, and a new turn starts. At the start of turn-jj, j=2,…,Mj=2,\ldots,M, the prefiller immediately generates Yj−1Y_{j-1} KV blocks for the response to the last prompt from turn-(j−1)(j-1), and XjX_{j} KV blocks for the new prompt of turn-jj. Then the corresponding KV blocks are transferred to the decoder, to generate the turn-jj response. Again, the tokens of this response, but not the KV blocks, are sent back to the prefiller. This marks the end of turn-jj. Therefore, the KV block increment of turn-jj ZjZ_{j} is defined by Z1:=X1​ and ​Zj:=Yj−1+Xj,j≥2Z_{1}:=X_{1}~\text{ and }~Z_{j}:=Y_{j-1}+X_{j},j\geq 2, where we assume Zj∈ℕ+Z_{j}\in\mathbb{N}_{+}. The history block size immediately after the turn-jj prompt is therefore defined as Rj:=∑ℓ=1jZℓR_{j}:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{j}Z_{\ell}. Fig. 1(a) illustrates the growth of the KV content. In Fig. 1, we use a running example to better illustrate the model setting.

Our analytical results for the MCM are established under the following additional assumptions. First, the turn-wise block increments {Zj}j≥1\{Z_{j}\}_{j\geq 1}, the interarrival times WW between each turn, and the turn number MM are mutually independent, while dependence across block increments of different turns is allowed. In addition, the cumulative number of KV blocks generated at the last turn of a conversation, defined as

B:=RM=∑ℓ=1MZℓ,B:=R_{M}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}Z_{\ell}, (1)

satisfies 𝔼⁡[exp⁡(θ0​B)]<∞\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta_{0}B)]<\infty for some θ0>0\theta_{0}>0. Finally, the interarrival time WW of prompts within one conversation has a Lipschitz continuous cumulative distribution function (CDF) FF.

The least-recently-used policy and the hit ratio.

Consider a generic conversation with MM turns and history content sizes {Rj}j=1M\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M}. If the conversation continues from turn jj to turn j+1j+1, then the RjR_{j} history blocks become reuse-eligible at the next prompt, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). If any prefix block cannot be recovered when its next-turn prompt arrives, all suffix blocks of this prefix block cannot be retrieved from the HBM33 3 In reality, these suffix blocks must be retrieved from lower-level storage or reprefilled, which causes more computation and transfer cost than the local HBM reuse. .

The MCM under our consideration operates under the LRU policy. The system maintains an ordered resident conversation list ℒ\mathcal{L}, from the most-recently-used (MRU) end to the LRU end. The list is updated whenever a new prompt is processed and the corresponding conversation content is inserted or refreshed in HBM. Suppose an arriving prompt belongs to a resident conversation θ∈ℒ\theta\in\mathcal{L}. The conversation label θ\theta is moved to the MRU end, while its previously stored content history is replaced by the enlarged content containing the newly generated blocks. If the prompt belongs to a nonresident conversation θ∉ℒ\theta\notin\mathcal{L}, the conversation is inserted directly at the MRU end, together with its available history content and the newly generated blocks.

The HBM can store at most NN KV blocks. Whenever inserting or updating a conversation content causes the total resident KV blocks to exceed this capacity, the system evicts complete conversation contents sequentially from the LRU end until the capacity constraint is restored44 4 In practical implementations, LRU eviction may operate at the block level and therefore allow partial-prefix eviction. We discuss these implementation differences in the appendix.. The whole-content LRU policy under our consideration is described by Algorithm 1 in the Appendix, and the hit ratio under LRU admits the following definition. For each turn j≥2j\geq 2, define the LRU hit indicator

Hj:=𝟙​{the history content of size Rj−1 is resident in HBM when the turn-j prompt arrives}.H_{j}:=\mathds{1}\left\{\text{the history content of size $R_{j-1}$ is resident in HBM when the turn-$j$ prompt arrives}\right\}.

The cache hit ratio is defined as h:=𝔼⁡[∑j=2MRj−1​Hj]/ARh:=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{j=2}^{M}R_{j-1}H_{j}]/{A_{R}}, where AR:=𝔼⁡[∑j=1MRj]A_{R}:=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{j=1}^{M}R_{j}] represents the expected cumulative history content workload over the lifetime of a conversation, and the numerator represents the portion of this workload that is reused through direct HBM lookup.

The mean-field asymptotic regime.

An explicit characterization of the hit ratio hh is rendered intractable due to the complex system dynamics, so we resort to a mean-field scaling regime where the conversation arrival rate scales proportionally with the HBM capacity NN, and we characterize the mean-field limit of the hit ratios. Specifically, the system indexed by NN has HBM capacity NN and conversation arrival rate λ0(N):=N​λ0\lambda_{0}^{(N)}:=N\lambda_{0}. The other system primitives, i.e., the prompt interarrival-time distribution FF, the turn-number distribution MM, and the block-increment sequence {(Xj,Yj)}j≥1\{(X_{j},Y_{j})\}_{j\geq 1}, are kept unchanged. Under this scaling, both the HBM capacity and the aggregate workload arrival rate grow linearly with NN, and we will show in the following section that this scaling yields a nondegenerate mean-field limit for the hit ratio.

3 Main results

In this section, we present our main theoretical result. We establish the convergence of the hit ratios for a sequence of MCMs operating under LRU and indexed by their HBM capacities N=1,2,…N=1,2,\ldots. Based on the mean-field convergence results, we develop a theoretically-motivated estimator for the hit ratio, and we validate its accuracy through real LLM serving experiments. For more details, we refer our readers to Appendix C. All proofs in this paper appear in Appendix D.

We consider the normalized displacement process of a tagged conversation, i.e., the cumulative KV block mass (normalized by N ) inserted or refreshed ahead of the tagged content in the LRU order since its last access. To state the main result, we define the mean displacement curve d:ℝ+→ℝ+d:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}, which is shown to be the mean of the normalized displacement process (see Lemma D.4), as

Note that dd is strictly increasing, and has a well-defined inverse d−1d^{-1}. We then define the mean-field characteristic time TC:=d−1​(1)T_{C}:=d^{-1}(1), i.e., the time at which the mass fills the entire cache.

We are now ready to state the main result. For the system indexed by NN, we let h(N)h^{(N)} denote the hit ratio and define the mean-field hit ratio as h(∞):=(AH/AR)​F​(TC)=(𝔼⁡[∑j=1M−1Rj]/𝔼⁡[∑j=1MRj])​F​(TC)h^{(\infty)}:=(A_{H}/{A_{R}})F(T_{C})=(\mathbb{E}[\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}R_{j}]/\mathbb{E}[\sum_{j=1}^{M}R_{j}])F(T_{C}).

Under the MCM assumptions, we have h(N)→h(∞)h^{(N)}\rightarrow h^{(\infty)} as N→∞.N\rightarrow\infty.

theoretically-motivated hit ratio estimator.

In real multi-turn LLM conversation systems, the last KV block generated at each turn is usually partially filled, which cannot be reused. We then modify the MCM to a practical version, where we further assume that the last block of each turn is partially filled and hence unhashable for prefix matching. Excluding one such block per non-final turn gives the expected reusable workload AHhash:=AH−𝔼⁡[M−1].A_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}:=A_{H}-\mathbb{E}[M-1]. h^:=A^Hhash/A^R​F^​(T^Cprac),\widehat{h}:={\widehat{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}}/{\widehat{A}_{R}}\,\widehat{F}(\widehat{T}_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}}), (3)

4 LLM Serving Experiments

In this section, we validate our estimator (3) using public multi-turn ShareGPT conversations (ShareGPT (2026)). Because each trace contains both prompts and responses, we use Prefill-Decode disaggregation to avoid inconsistencies between the generated responses and subsequent recorded prompts. We deploy Qwen3-8B on 5 Ascend 910B2 NPUs, with one NPU as the prefiller. We assign 40 GB of prefiller HBM for the KV cache, such that the block capacity is N=2,275N=2,275. We use 5,000 conversations for measurement under Poisson conversation arrivals. More details on the experimental setting are deferred to Appendix E.

In Experiment 1, we fix λ0=1.5\lambda_{0}=1.5 and vary the target mean prompt interarrival time μF\mu_{F}, using an exponential clock. However, a new prompt is submitted when both the sampled exponential clock rings and the previous decoding finishes. The prior estimator uses F⁡(t)=1−e​x​p​(−tμF)F(t)=1-exp(-\frac{t}{\mu_{F}}), while the posterior estimator replaces μF\mu_{F} by the measured mean interarrival time μ^F\hat{\mu}_{F}. We report the absolute error AE=|estimated hit ratio−actual hit ratio|\mathrm{AE}=|\text{estimated hit ratio}-\text{actual hit ratio}| and relative error RE=AE/actual hit ratio×100%\mathrm{RE}=\mathrm{AE}/\text{actual hit ratio}\times 100\%. In Experiment 2, we fix μF=135\mu_{F}=135s, under which μ^F\hat{\mu}_{F} is closest to the target, and vary the conversation arrival rate from 0.50.5 to 2.02.0. Results are shown in Figs. 3, 4, 5 and 6. Both estimators capture the decrease in empirical hit ratio when either μF\mu_{F} or the λ0\lambda_{0} increases. In addition, the AE remains below 0.020.02, and the RE is below 10%10\% when the realized interarrival time closely matches its target.

5 Conclusion

We studied the characterization of the hit ratio in LLM serving systems with multi-turn conversations. We proposed a parsimonious multi-turn conversation model under the widely adopted least-recently-used policy, which captures several key components governing the real system dynamics. Through a mean-field asymptotic framework, we proved the convergence of the hit ratios to a certain mean-field hit ratio limit as the HBM capacity N→∞N\to\infty. Based on our characterization of the mean-field limit, we designed a hit ratio estimator for practical LLM serving systems, and validated its accuracy via LLM serving experiments with the Qwen3-8B model implemented on Ascend 910B2 NPUs. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for analyzing multi-turn LLM services, and provides practical system-design guidelines on memory provisioning that achieves a target hit ratio.

Appendix A Prior Work

A.1 Caching Systems and KV-Cache Management for Multi-turn LLM Serving

Recent caching systems reveal several workload characteristics that are particularly relevant to multi-turn LLM serving. In conventional caching systems, some caches’ highly heterogeneous object sizes have already been observed in production workloads and incorporated into cache admission and resource allocation (Berger et al. [2017], Berger et al. [2018], Berg et al. [2020]). In LLM serving, KV states are typically managed at the block level (Kwon et al. [2023]), while block reuse may span multiple conversation turns and even multiple storage tiers (DeepSeek [2024], Gao et al. [2024], Qin et al. [2025]). Production traces further show substantial heterogeneity in KV-cache reuse intervals, reuse probabilities, and reusable prefix lengths across requests Wang et al. [2025]. Practical serving platforms therefore employ mechanisms such as LRU- or priority-based eviction, prefix matching, and KV-aware routing under limited cache capacity (Thomson et al. [2025]). Moreover, a distinctive feature of multi-turn LLM workloads is that the cacheable blocks associated with the same conversation grow across successive accesses, rather than remaining a fixed-size object.

A.2 Previous Analyses of LRU and Hit Ratio

We now review prior analytical work on the least-recently-used (LRU) cache management policy. Existing analyses have mainly focused on web and content caching systems, where a fixed population of cacheable objects is repeatedly requested according to independent, stationary, or temporally correlated request processes. A common objective is to characterize the miss or hit probability of LRU in large-cache regimes, often through asymptotic approximations that replace the complicated LRU ordering dynamics with a more tractable working-set or time-to-live (TTL) representation. One of the earliest asymptotic analyses of LRU can be found in Fagin [1977], which showed that the expected LRU miss ratio can be asymptotically approximated by the miss ratio of a corresponding working-set model. This working-set model characterizes cache residency through a fixed window of recent page references. A closely related line of work analyzes LRU through a deterministic characteristic time that approximates the random eviction time of a cached object. Che et al. [2002] introduced this characteristic time approximation for hierarchical web caches, which was later widely referred to as the Che approximation. A mathematical explanation for its accuracy was provided in Fricker et al. [2012] by relating the eviction of a tagged object to the cumulative number of distinct objects requested after its last access. In Martina et al. [2014], this characteristic time decoupling principle was further extended to general renewal traffic, multiple cache management policies, and interconnected caches. Subsequent work established stronger asymptotic foundations for characteristic time and TTL approximations under more general request processes, including shot-noise request models with temporal locality (Leonardi and Torrisi [2017]) and independent stationary and ergodic request processes (Jiang et al. [2018]). In addition, Gast and Van Houdt [2017] connected TTL approximations for LRU variants to deterministic transient mean-field ODE limits under the IRM, whose fixed points recover the proposed TTL approximations.

Our analysis builds on a similar general principle. We represent LRU eviction through the cumulative workload that moves ahead of a tagged conversation content and identify a deterministic characteristic time in the mean-field limit. However, multi-turn LLM conversations introduce several challenges that are absent from previous theoretical work, which focuses on traditional object-based caching models. First, cacheable KV blocks have finite reuse lifetimes. A block can only be reused by subsequent turns of its corresponding conversation. Once the conversation terminates, its blocks may still occupy HBM but can never generate another cache hit. Moreover, the server does not know in advance when a conversation will terminate, which contrasts with classical IRM settings with a fixed population of objects and time-invariant request probabilities. Second, the reusable history associated with a conversation grows over time, so a later access can touch a nondecreasing number of KV blocks. As a result, the displacement process must track the amount of KV block workload moved ahead of the tagged content, while the size of the tagged content itself is also random and increases with the turn state. Finally, request-level hit probability is insufficient for quantifying cache effectiveness in LLM serving because different prompts may reuse substantially different numbers of historical KV blocks. Inspired by the byte hit ratio used in content delivery network (Berger et al. [2017]), we therefore define a hit ratio that weights successful reuse by the number of KV blocks served from HBM, which further quantifies the computational and data-movement savings benefited by LRU caching.

Appendix B Model details and formal definitions

In this section, we formulate the multi-turn conversation model (MCM) and introduce the whole-content Least-Recently Used (LRU) policy. We begin with basic notation in Section B.1. In Section B.2, we define the MCM for multi-turn LLM inference. We then introduce the hit ratio and characterize its intrinsic upper bound in Section B.3. In Section B.4, we specify the whole-content LRU policy used in our theoretical analysis. The mean-field scaling is introduced in Section B.5. Finally, in Section B.6, we define the tagged-conversation displacement process and its characteristic time. These two terms will be used as the key stochastic objects in our mean-field analysis in Appendix C. Their limiting behavior is important for our subsequent hit ratio convergence analysis.

B.1 Basic Notations

We let ℕ\mathbb{N} denote the set of nonnegative integers and ℕ+\mathbb{N}_{+} denote the set of positive integers. For a cumulative distribution function FF, its survival function is defined as F¯\bar{F} with F¯​(t):=1−F​(t)\bar{F}(t):=1-F(t).

B.2 Multi-Turn Conversation Model

We first introduce our multi-turn conversation model (MCM). In LLM practice, KVs are managed as blocks in the system, the number of which can be modeled to follow some integer distribution. For instance, in our experiment, 128 tokens are arranged in a block, which always has a constant memory requirement. We consider a system with an HBM KV block memory capacity N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, i.e., the HBM can store at most NN KV blocks. New conversations arrive according to a Poisson process of rate λ0\lambda_{0}. Each conversation enters the system and immediately produces a prompt corresponding to X1X_{1} KV blocks, and the LLM generates a sentence corresponding to Y1Y_{1} KV blocks. We assume that the number of turns of a conversation follows some positive integer distribution MM. At turn-jj, the numbers of prompt blocks and response blocks generated follow a joint distribution (Xj,Yj)∈ℕ2(X_{j},Y_{j})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}.

Our model is motivated by the Prefill-Decode disaggregation setting, where the KV block composition at successive turns is visualized in Fig. 1(a). We define the turn-wise content increment as Z1:=X1Z_{1}:=X_{1} and

Zj:=Xj+Yj−1,j≥2.Z_{j}:=X_{j}+Y_{j-1},\qquad j\geq 2.

We assume Zj∈ℕ+Z_{j}\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, so that every turn increases the history content by at least one KV block. The history content size immediately after the turn-jj prompt is therefore defined as

Rj:=∑ℓ=1jZℓ=∑ℓ=1jXℓ+∑ℓ=1j−1Yℓ.R_{j}:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{j}Z_{\ell}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{j}X_{\ell}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{j-1}Y_{\ell}. (4)

Thus, RjR_{j} contains all prompt KV blocks up to turn jj and all response KV blocks generated up to turn j−1j-1. This entire history content is required to process the turn-jj prompt and generate the corresponding response.

A running example.

Fig. 1(b) illustrates a running example of how KV blocks in one turn are managed. Lowercase letters denote tokens, and uppercase letters denote block numbers. The tokens at the start of turn-33 are (x1,y1,x2,y2,x3)(x_{1},y_{1},x_{2},y_{2},x_{3}). All history KV blocks (or “prefix KV blocks”) (X1,Y1,X2)(X_{1},Y_{1},X_{2}) are retrieved and reused from HBM, based on which the prefiller generates Y2Y_{2} KV blocks for the response y2y_{2} from the last turn, and X3X_{3} blocks for the new prompt x3x_{3}. All KV blocks (X1,Y1,X2,Y2,X3)(X_{1},Y_{1},X_{2},Y_{2},X_{3}) are passed to a decoder to generate the new response y3y_{3} for the prompt x3x_{3}. But only the tokens y3y_{3}, not the KV blocks Y3Y_{3}, are sent back to the prefiller for turn-44’s compute.

Remark B.1.

The treatment of response KV blocks may differ across several state-of-the-art LLM serving architectures. The HBM KV block increment dynamics described above are most relevant in the Prefill-Decode disaggregation architecture in which response KV blocks are released after decoding. In this case, when the conversation receives the next-turn prompt, the corresponding response history must be reconstructed on the prefill side.

Under some Prefill-Decode disaggregation frameworks, however, response KV blocks may be transferred back to the prefill-side worker through a “write-back" mechanism and retained for future reuse. Similarly, when prefilling and decoding are operated on the same processing unit, the newly generated response KV blocks may remain directly resident in HBM. Nevertheless, in either case, the alternative architecture can be accommodated by redefining the turn-wise increment ZjZ_{j} and the turn boundary.

Our MCM is constructed under the following assumptions.

Assumption B.2 (Independent Block Increments).

The block-increment pairs {(Xj,Yj)}j≥1\{(X_{j},Y_{j})\}_{j\geq 1} (allowing arbitrary dependence across turns) are independent of the total number of turns MM within a conversation. The turn-wise content increments ZiZ_{i} satisfy that Zi≥1Z_{i}\geq 1 for all i≥1i\geq 1.

Assumption B.3 (Light-tailed Cumulative Block Workload).

The cumulative number of KV blocks generated over the lifetime of a conversation, defined as

B:=RM=∑ℓ=1MZℓ,B:=R_{M}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}Z_{\ell}, (5)

has a finite moment generating function in a positive neighborhood of 00, i.e., there exists θ0>0\theta_{0}>0 such that 𝔼⁡[eθ0​B]<∞\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta_{0}B}]<\infty.

Assumption B.4 (i.i.d. Prompt Interarrival Times with a Lipschitz-continuous CDF.).

For each conversation, let WjW_{j} denote the interarrival time between the submissions of the turn-jj prompt and the turn-(j+1)(j+1) prompt. The sequence {Wj}j≥1\{W_{j}\}_{j\geq 1} is assumed to be i.i.d. with cumulative distribution function (CDF) FF, independent of MM and the block increments {(Xj,Yj)}j≥1\{(X_{j},Y_{j})\}_{j\geq 1}. We further assume that FF is Lipschitz-continuous with constant LFL_{F} and μF:=𝔼⁡[W]<∞\mu_{F}:=\mathbb{E}[W]<\infty.

We note that the MCM reduces to the stochastic conversation model (SCM) introduced in Zhang et al. [2025], under the following additional assumptions:

  1. 1.

    The block-increment pairs {(Xj,Yj)}j≥1\{(X_{j},Y_{j})\}_{j\geq 1} are i.i.d.;

  2. 2.

    The prompt interarrival times are i.i.d. exponentially distributed with rate r>0r>0;

  3. 3.

    The total number of turns MM is geometrically distributed. Specifically, after each completed turn, a conversation continues with probability p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) and terminates with probability q:=1−pq:=1-p. Equivalently, an active conversation can be viewed as having an independent new-prompt Poisson clock with rate p​rpr and an independent termination Poisson clock with rate q​rqr.

When the block increments additionally have constant means 𝔼⁡[Xj]=k\mathbb{E}[X_{j}]=k and 𝔼⁡[Yj]=m\mathbb{E}[Y_{j}]=m for all j≥1j\geq 1, the expected history content size after turn jj can be simplified as

R¯j:=𝔼⁡[Rj]=j​k+(j−1)​m.\bar{R}_{j}:=\mathbb{E}[R_{j}]=jk+(j-1)m.

B.3 The Hit Ratio

We next introduce the hit ratio, which measures the cache reuse effectiveness of a management policy and will serve as the main performance metric throughout the paper. Unlike a request-level hit ratio that assigns equal weight to each cache access, the hit ratio quantifies the fraction of the overall KV block workload that can be directly served through history reuse from HBM. This block-level metric is particularly important for multi-turn LLM serving, because different conversations, and even different turns within the same conversation, may have substantially different history lengths.

Consider a generic conversation with MM turns and history content sizes {Rj}j=1M\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M}. If the conversation continues from turn jj to turn j+1j+1, then the RjR_{j} history blocks become reuse-eligible at the next prompt. Ideally, these blocks can be retrieved directly from HBM rather than reconstructed through reprefilling or transferred from lower-level storage such as CPU DRAM or SSD. Before decoding the turn-(j+1)(j+1) response, the previously generated history and the newly arrived turn-(j+1)(j+1) prompt must be organized as the complete prefix required by the model. We note that, on the one hand, recovering missing history from lower-level storage introduces additional communication and storage overhead. On the other hand, reprefilling the corresponding tokens incurs additional computation and increases the workload on the prefiller. In contrast, directly reusing resident KV blocks from HBM can reduce both data transfer overhead and recomputation cost. This motivates a workload-level metric that captures the amount of reusable KV history served from HBM.

We next specify the conditions under which a KV block stored in HBM can be successfully reused when its corresponding conversation receives a new prompt. In practical prefix-caching systems, two conditions are generally required:

  1. 1.

    The block must be fully populated and therefore hashable, which means that its complete token content can be mapped to a deterministic identifier (a hash value) and stored in a hash map for later exact prefix matching and lookup. For instance, in our experiments (see Appendix E), each block corresponds to 128128 tokens. A block having less than 128128 tokens becomes an unhashed block and cannot be reused. Such a phenomenon happens because the block is from the tail of a conversation and cannot fill a block.

  2. 2.

    All preceding blocks in the same prefix must also be available55 5 However, the preceding blocks do not necessarily need to reside in HBM. They may instead be retrieved from lower-level storage, such as CPU DRAM or SSD. After finding these prefix blocks, the subsequent blocks that remain resident in HBM can still be reused., because cache reuse follows the prefix-hit rule. For example, suppose a conversation contains blocks indexed from 00 to 66. Even if block-55 is fully populated and resident in HBM, it cannot be reused if block-44 is unavailable in any storage. In this case, block-55 must be reprefilled together with the missing preceding blocks.

In our theoretical MCM analysis, we assume that all KV blocks are fully populated and hence hashable, so that condition 1 is always satisfied. The effect of unhashable tail blocks will be incorporated later in our practical MCM. We now define the hit ratio.

Definition B.5.

For each turn j≥2j\geq 2, let the random variable RjH∈ℕR^{H}_{j}\in\mathbb{N} denote the stationary number of history-prefix blocks reused directly from HBM under the LRU policy by a turn-jj access, with 0≤RjH≤Rj−10\leq R^{H}_{j}\leq R_{j-1}. The hit ratio under LRU is defined as

h:=𝔼⁡[∑j=2MRjH]𝔼⁡[∑j=1MRj].h:=\frac{\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum\limits_{j=2}^{M}R^{H}_{j}\Big]}{\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum\limits_{j=1}^{M}R_{j}\Big]}. (6)

In (6), the denominator 𝔼⁡[∑j=1MRj]\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum\limits_{j=1}^{M}R_{j}\Big] represents the expected cumulative history content workload over the lifetime of a conversation, whereas the numerator represents the portion of this workload that is successfully touched through direct HBM reuse.

We use a simple example to illustrate this definition. Suppose a conversation contains three turns, with X1=2X_{1}=2, X2=4X_{2}=4, Y1=2Y_{1}=2, Y2=5Y_{2}=5, and X3=3X_{3}=3. Then the history content sizes are R1=X1=2R_{1}=X_{1}=2, R2=X1+(X2+Y1)=8R_{2}=X_{1}+(X_{2}+Y_{1})=8, and R3=X1+(X2+Y1)+(X3+Y2)=16R_{3}=X_{1}+(X_{2}+Y_{1})+(X_{3}+Y_{2})=16. Suppose that, under LRU, all history blocks required at turns 2 and 3 are successfully reused from HBM. Then the hit ratio is

h=0+2+82+8+16=1026.h=\frac{0+2+8}{2+8+16}=\frac{10}{26}.

A key feature of the hit ratio is that its intrinsic upper bound is usually strictly smaller than 11. This is because newly arrived prompt blocks cannot be reused from HBM, and only history contents associated with conversations that continue to the next turn are eligible for reuse. We therefore characterize the maximum upper bound on the hit ratio.

Define the sequence of tail probabilities

Sj:=ℙ⁡(M≥j),j≥1,S_{j}:=\mathbb{P}(M\geq j),\qquad j\geq 1, (7)

where S1=1S_{1}=1 and Sj↓0S_{j}\downarrow 0. For every jj such that Sj>0S_{j}>0, define

pj:=ℙ⁡(M≥j+1∣M≥j)=Sj+1Sj,p_{j}:=\mathbb{P}(M\geq j+1\mid M\geq j)=\frac{S_{j+1}}{S_{j}}, (8)

as the continuation probability at turn-jj, and qj:=1−pjq_{j}:=1-p_{j} as the corresponding termination probability. The expected cumulative history content workload over a conversation lifetime is

AR:=𝔼⁡[∑j=1MRj]=∑j≥1Sj​R¯j,A_{R}:=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum\limits_{j=1}^{M}R_{j}\right]=\sum_{j\geq 1}S_{j}\bar{R}_{j}, (9)

whereas the expected amount of reusable history content workload is

AH:=𝔼⁡[∑j=1M−1Rj]=∑j≥1Sj+1​R¯j.A_{H}:=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum\limits_{j=1}^{M-1}R_{j}\right]=\sum_{j\geq 1}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j}. (10)

We define the intrinsic reuse potential of the workload as

hmax:=AHAR.h_{\max}:=\frac{A_{H}}{A_{R}}. (11)

Then, for any HBM capacity,

h≤hmax.h\leq h_{\max}.

The quantity hmaxh_{\max} depends only on the statistical structure of the multi-turn conversation workload and is independent of the cache-management policy or the conversation-prompt arrival dynamics.

For instance, in our SCM model, where pj≡pp_{j}\equiv p, qj≡1−pq_{j}\equiv 1-p, and R¯j=j​k+(j−1)​m\bar{R}_{j}=jk+(j-1)m, we have that AR=k+p​mq2A_{R}=\frac{k+pm}{q^{2}} and AH=p⁡(k+p​m)q2A_{H}=\frac{p(k+pm)}{q^{2}}. Hence, the intrinsic reuse potential has a closed form hmax=ph_{\max}=p, which only depends on the continuation probability, or equivalently the mean number of turns in a conversation.

B.4 The Least-Recently-Used (LRU) Policy

In our MCM, we consider a whole-content version of the least-recently-used (LRU) policy. The system maintains an ordered resident list ℒ\mathcal{L}, from the most-recently-used (MRU) end to the LRU end. The list is updated whenever a new prompt is processed and the corresponding conversation content is inserted or refreshed in HBM. Suppose an arriving prompt belongs to a resident conversation θ∈ℒ\theta\in\mathcal{L}. The conversation label θ\theta is removed from its current position and moved to the MRU end, while its previously stored content is replaced by the enlarged content containing the newly generated blocks. If the prompt belongs to a nonresident conversation θ∉ℒ\theta\notin\mathcal{L}, the conversation is inserted directly at the MRU end, together with its available history content and the newly generated blocks.

As specified in Section B.2, the HBM can store at most NN KV blocks. Whenever inserting or updating a conversation content causes the total resident KV block workload to exceed this capacity, the system will evict complete conversation contents sequentially from the LRU end until the capacity constraint is restored.66 6 In practical implementations, LRU eviction may operate at the block level and therefore allow partial-prefix eviction. We discuss these implementation differences in Appendix E. The whole-content LRU policy under our consideration is described by Algorithm 1 below.

Under the whole-content LRU policy in our MCM, a conversation content is either fully resident in HBM or entirely absent. If the content is missed when its next-turn prompt arrives, its history blocks must be retrieved from lower-level storage or reconstructed through reprefilling. Therefore, the hit ratio admits the following equivalent characterization.

For each turn j≥2j\geq 2, define the LRU hit indicator

Hj:=𝟙​{the history content of size Rj−1 is resident in HBM when turn j arrives}.H_{j}:=\mathds{1}\left\{\text{the history content of size $R_{j-1}$ is resident in HBM when turn $j$ arrives}\right\}.

If Hj=1H_{j}=1, all Rj−1R_{j-1} history blocks can be directly reused from HBM. Otherwise, none of these blocks is touched through HBM reuse under the whole-content convention. Hence, the hit ratio in (6) can be equivalently written as

h:=𝔼⁡[∑j=2MRj−1​Hj]𝔼⁡[∑j=1MRj].h:=\frac{\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum\limits_{j=2}^{M}R_{j-1}H_{j}\Big]}{\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum\limits_{j=1}^{M}R_{j}\Big]}. (12)

B.5 The Mean-Field Asymptotic Regime

We next introduce the mean-field scaling used in our theoretical analysis. The motivation is that, if the HBM capacity NN is very large while the conversation arrival process remains unchanged, an arriving prompt can retain almost all reusable history blocks in HBM, and the hit ratio approaches the upper bound hmaxh_{\max}. Similarly, when NN is very small, only a negligible fraction of the history workload can remain resident in HBM, and the hit ratio approaches 00. To obtain a nontrivial asymptotic regime, we therefore scale the conversation arrival rate proportionally with the HBM capacity.

Specifically, for the system indexed by NN, we set

λ0(N):=N​λ0,\lambda_{0}^{(N)}:=N\lambda_{0},

while keeping the prompt interarrival distribution FF, the turn-number distribution MM, and the block-increment sequence {(Xj,Yj)}j≥1\{(X_{j},Y_{j})\}_{j\geq 1} unchanged. Under this scaling, both the HBM capacity and the aggregate workload arrival rate grow linearly with NN, and we will show in Section C.1 that this scaling yields a nondegenerate mean-field limit for the cache dynamics and hit ratio.

Remark B.6.

The mean-field scaling above has an equivalent interpretation obtained through a rescaling of prompt interarrival time. Specifically, suppose that we keep the conversation arrival rate fixed at λ0\lambda_{0}, while scaling the prompt interarrival distribution as F(N)(⋅):=F(⋅/N)F^{(N)}(\cdot):=F(\cdot/N), i.e., the original interarrival times are scaled by a factor of NN. Under the scaled time t:=t/Nt:=t/N, conversations then arrive at rate N​λ0N\lambda_{0}, while the interarrival distribution becomes FF, which is exactly the mean-field scaling considered above.

This alternative interpretation is closer to our LLM inference experiments. In practice, increasing the physical conversation arrival rate proportionally with NN may overload the prefill and decode workers and make computation be the system bottleneck. The resulting end-to-end (E2E) latency may then substantially affect the observed prompt interarrival times. Therefore, we use the arrival-rate scaling λ0(N)=N​λ0\lambda_{0}^{(N)}=N\lambda_{0} for the theoretical mean-field analysis. Nonetheless, in the experiments we keep the physical conversation arrival rate at a practical level and adjust the prompt interarrival times to emulate the corresponding mean-field regime.

B.6 Tagged-conversation Displacement Process and Characteristic Time

Our mean-field analysis uses a classical tagged-job approach in queueing theory. In our setting, we tag a conversation immediately after its turn-jj access and study its subsequent evolution in stationarity. We introduce two key notions: the tagged-conversation displacement process and the corresponding characteristic time. These objects provide the basis for our mean-field analysis of eviction and the LRU hit ratio.

We first formulate a tagged-conversation representation of the whole-content LRU dynamics. The key idea is to characterize the eviction of a tagged content through the cumulative KV block mass that moves ahead of it, after its most recent access. This transforms the evolution of the LRU ordering into a one-dimensional cumulative displacement process.

We tag a conversation immediately after one of its prompt accesses. Suppose that the tagged conversation receives its turn-jj prompt at time 00 and is moved to the MRU end of the whole-content LRU list. At this moment, no other resident blocks lie ahead of the tagged content in the LRU ordering. Assuming that the tagged conversation receives no further access before eviction, as other conversations are subsequently accessed, their KV blocks move to the MRU side and therefore accumulate in front of the tagged content.

A background conversation that has already moved ahead of the tagged content should not contribute its entire content again at its later accesses. Once its pre-existing history has crossed the tagged content, only the newly appended KV blocks generated at subsequent accesses further increase the block mass ahead of the tagged content. Hence, for each background conversation ii, define its cumulative displacement contribution Ci​(t)C_{i}(t) as follows:

  1. 1.

    Before its first access after time 00, Ci​(t)=0C_{i}(t)=0;

  2. 2.

    At its first access after time 00, its complete pre-existing history content and the newly accessed prompt’s blocks cross the tagged content;

  3. 3.

    At each subsequent access, only the newly appended KV block mass contributes additional displacement.

We are now ready to define the tagged-conversation displacement process.

Definition B.7 ((Tagged Turn-jj Conversation) Displacement Process).

In the MCM-LRU system with HBM capacity NN, consider a tagged conversation immediately after its turn-jj access at time 00, with history content size RjR_{j}. We condition on the event that its content is evicted before its next reuse. The displacement process of this content immediately after its turn-jj access is defined as

DN,j​(t):=∑i≠tagCi​(t),t≥0.D_{N,j}(t):=\sum_{i\neq\mathrm{tag}}C_{i}(t),\qquad t\geq 0. (13)

The corresponding normalized displacement process is defined as DN,j​(t)N\frac{D_{N,j}(t)}{N}.

Under the whole-content LRU convention, DN,j​(t)D_{N,j}(t) is nondecreasing in tt. We next define the corresponding characteristic time, denoted by τC(N)​(j)\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j).

Definition B.8 (Tagged Turn-jj Characteristic Time).

Consider a tagged conversation immediately after its turn-jj access at time 00, with history content size RjR_{j}. We condition on the event that its content is evicted before its next reuse. The characteristic time τC(N)​(j)\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j) is defined as the time required for the background displacement to evict this tagged content from HBM, assuming that the tagged conversation is not accessed again before eviction. Specifically,

τC(N)(j):={0,Rj>N,inf{t≥0:DN,j​(t)>N−Rj},Rj≤N.\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j):=\begin{cases}0,&R_{j}>N,\\ \inf\{t\geq 0:D_{N,j}(t)>N-R_{j}\},&R_{j}\leq N.\end{cases} (14)

In Section C.1, we establish the convergence of the normalized displacement process DN,j​(t)N\frac{D_{N,j}(t)}{N} and the characteristic time τC(N)​(j)\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j), and then use these results to derive the mean-field convergence of the LRU hit ratio.

Appendix C Extended mean-field results

In this section, we present the main theoretical results of our mean-field analysis. We first establish the convergence of the displacement process, the characteristic time, and the LRU hit ratio for the multi-turn conversation model (MCM) in Section C.1. In Section C.2, we extend the analysis to a practical MCM that incorporates additional features of real multi-turn LLM serving systems. Based on its mean-field convergence results, we develop a theoretically-motivated estimator for the hit ratio. The accuracy of this estimator will be evaluated empirically in Appendix E. Unless otherwise stated, all results in this section concern a stationary system.

C.1 Mean-Field Results of the MCM under LRU

We begin with the mean-field limit of the (tagged-conversation) displacement process. Its normalized sample path converges uniformly on every finite time horizon to the deterministic mean displacement curve. We first define this mean displacement curve.

Definition C.1.

Recall that AH:=∑j≥1Sj+1​R¯jA_{H}:=\sum_{j\geq 1}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j} denotes the expected amount of history content workload eligible for reuse, and that B:=RMB:=R_{M} denotes the total KV block count required by the end of a conversation. Theorem C.2 (Sample-Path Convergence of the Normalized Displacement Process).

The tagged turn-jj content process follows the same law, such that DN,j​(⋅)​=𝑑​DN​(⋅)D_{N,j}(\cdot)\overset{d}{=}D_{N}(\cdot) for every turn state jj. Then, for every t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and every ε>0\varepsilon>0,

ℙ⁡(|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|>ε)≤VTN​ε2.\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq\frac{V_{T}}{N\varepsilon^{2}}. (16)

Moreover, for every 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1,

ℙ⁡(sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|>ε)≤CTN​ε3,\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq\frac{C_{T}}{N\varepsilon^{3}}, (17)

where CT:=16​VT9​(2+4​L​T).C_{T}:=\frac{16V_{T}}{9}(2+4LT).
