sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|→ℙ0.\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0. (18)

In particular, the finite-size bounds imply

|DN​(t)N−d(t)|=Oℙ(N−1/2)\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|=O_{\mathbb{P}}(N^{-1/2}) (19)

for every fixed tt, and

sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d(t)|=Oℙ(N−1/3).\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|=O_{\mathbb{P}}(N^{-1/3}). (20)

We defer the proof of Theorem C.2 to Section D.1. Nonetheless, we provide a proof sketch.

Proof Sketch: We first represent the stationary background conversations as a marked Poisson random measure. Hence, we can express the displacement process as an integral of their cumulative displacement contributions. This representation also shows that the law of the background displacement process is invariant w.r.t. the tagged turn state jj. We then derive the mean displacement curve d⁡(t)d(t) by separately evaluating the expected contributions from pre-existing history contents and newly generated KV blocks. The Poisson random measure representation further yields a pointwise second-moment bound of order O⁡(N−1)O(N^{-1}) for the normalized displacement process. Finally, using the nondecreasing property of DN​(t)D_{N}(t) and d⁡(t)d(t), the Lipschitz continuity of d⁡(t)d(t), and a discretization argument over a finite time horizon with granularity O⁡(N13)O(N^{\frac{1}{3}}), we obtain the uniform convergence. □\square

The sample-path convergence of the displacement process leads to our next core result, the tagged turn-jj content characteristic time converges to a deterministic limit. We first define this limiting mean-field characteristic time. Recall from Definition C.1 that d⁡(0)=0d(0)=0 and d⁡(t)→∞d(t)\rightarrow\infty as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. Moreover, dd is differentiable with uniformly lower bounded derivative

d′​(t)=λ0​𝔼​[B]+λ0​AH​F¯​(t)≥λ0​𝔼​[B]>0.d^{\prime}(t)=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]+\lambda_{0}A_{H}\bar{F}(t)\geq\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]>0.

Hence, dd is strictly increasing, and its inverse d−1:[0,∞)→[0,∞)d^{-1}:[0,\infty)\rightarrow[0,\infty) is well-defined.

Definition C.3.

The mean-field characteristic time TCT_{C} is defined as TC:=d−1​(1)T_{C}:=d^{-1}(1), or equivalently, as the unique solution to the equation

d⁡(TC)=λ0​𝔼​[B]​TC+λ0​AH​∫0TCF¯​(u)​𝑑u=1.d(T_{C})=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]T_{C}+\lambda_{0}A_{H}\int_{0}^{T_{C}}\bar{F}(u)\,du=1. (21)

We now state our second core result on the convergence of the characteristic time.

Theorem C.4 (Characteristic Time Convergence).

Fix a turn state jj such that Sj>0S_{j}>0, and a finite horizon T>TCT>T_{C}. For every

0<ε<min⁡{TC,T−TC},0<\varepsilon<\min\{T_{C},T-T_{C}\},

the characteristic time satisfies

ℙ⁡(|τC(N)​(j)−TC|>ε)≤18​VTN​cd2​ε2+𝔼⁡[eθ​B]Sj​exp⁡(−θ​cd3​N​ε),\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)-T_{C}\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq\frac{18V_{T}}{Nc_{d}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta B}]}{S_{j}}\exp\left(-\frac{\theta c_{d}}{3}N\varepsilon\right), (22)

where cd:=λ0​𝔼​[B]c_{d}:=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B] and VT:=∫𝒵GT​(z)2​ν​(𝑑z)<∞V_{T}:=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}G_{T}(z)^{2}\,\nu(dz)<\infty is the second-moment constant introduced in Lemma D.1. Consequently,

τC(N)​(j)→ℙTC\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}T_{C} (23)

for every fixed turn state jj with Sj≥0S_{j}\geq 0, and

τC(N)(j)−TC=Oℙ(N−1/2).\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)-T_{C}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(N^{-1/2}).

The proof of Theorem C.4 is deferred to Section D.2. We also provide a proof sketch here.

Proof Sketch: We note that different tagged turn-jj contents have different eviction thresholds, because eviction occurs when DN,j​(t)>N−RjD_{N,j}(t)>N-R_{j}. However, for any fixed jj with Sj>0S_{j}>0, the content size satisfies Rj=Oℙ​(1)R_{j}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(1), and hence Rj/NR_{j}/N is asymptotically negligible. To control the event {|τC(N)(j)−TC|>ε}\{|\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)-T_{C}|>\varepsilon\}, it is sufficient to control the normalized displacement process at the two deterministic times TC−εT_{C}-\varepsilon and TC+εT_{C}+\varepsilon, and the deviation of Rj/NR_{j}/N from 00. Because d⁡(TC−ε)<1<d⁡(TC+ε)d(T_{C}-\varepsilon)<1<d(T_{C}+\varepsilon), the pointwise concentration bounds for |DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)||\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)| imply that, with high probability, the tagged content is resident at time TC−εT_{C}-\varepsilon and already evicted by time TC+εT_{C}+\varepsilon. By applying a union bound to these deviations, we obtain the convergence of τC(N)​(j)\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j) to TCT_{C}. The Oℙ(N−1/2)O_{\mathbb{P}}(N^{-1/2}) convergence rate follows from the pointwise concentration rate of the displacement process in Theorem C.2. □\square

We finally turn to the third core result for the MCM-LRU system: the convergence of the hit ratio. In the system indexed by NN, for each turn j≥2j\geq 2, define the hit indicator

HN,j:=𝟙​{the history content of size Rj−1 is resident in HBM when turn j arrives}.H_{N,j}:=\mathds{1}\left\{\text{the history content of size $R_{j-1}$ is resident in HBM when turn $j$ arrives}\right\}.

Then the finite-NN hit ratio under whole-content LRU can be written as

h(N):=𝔼⁡[∑j=1M−1Rj​HN,j+1]AR,h^{(N)}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}R_{j}H_{N,j+1}\right]}{A_{R}}, (24)

where we recall that AR=∑j≥1Sj​R¯j.A_{R}=\sum_{j\geq 1}S_{j}\bar{R}_{j}. We define the corresponding mean-field limiting hit ratio as

h(∞):=AHAR​F​(TC).h^{(\infty)}:=\frac{A_{H}}{A_{R}}F(T_{C}). (25)

We now state Theorem C.5, which follows from the convergence of the displacement process and the characteristic time established above. Its proof is deferred to Section D.3.

Theorem C.5 (Hit Ratio Convergence in the MCM-LRU Model).

Under the MCM assumptions, fix a finite JJ such that SJ+1>0S_{J+1}>0, and fix T>TCT>T_{C}. For every 0<ε<min⁡{TC,T−TC}0<\varepsilon<\min\{T_{C},T-T_{C}\},

|hLRU(N)−hLRU(∞)|≤LF​ε​AH(J)AR+KJAR​pN,J​(ε)+2​𝔼​[B2​eθ​B]​e−θ⁡(J+2)AR,\left|h_{\mathrm{LRU}}^{(N)}-h_{\mathrm{LRU}}^{(\infty)}\right|\leq\frac{L_{F}\varepsilon A_{H}^{(J)}}{A_{R}}+\frac{K_{J}}{A_{R}}\sqrt{p_{N,J}(\varepsilon)}+\frac{2\mathbb{E}[B^{2}e^{\theta B}]e^{-\theta(J+2)}}{A_{R}}, (26)

where pN,j​(ε):=18​VTN​cd2​ε2+𝔼⁡[eθ​B]Sj​exp⁡(−θ​cd3​N​ε)p_{N,j}(\varepsilon):=\frac{18V_{T}}{Nc_{d}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta B}]}{S_{j}}\exp\left(-\frac{\theta c_{d}}{3}N\varepsilon\right) and KJ:=∑j=1JSj+1​𝔼⁡[Rj2]K_{J}:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[R_{j}^{2}]}. Consequently, the system-level hit ratio under the whole-content LRU policy converges when N→∞N\rightarrow\infty:

hLRU(N)→hLRU(∞)=AHAR​F​(TC).h_{\mathrm{LRU}}^{(N)}\rightarrow h_{\mathrm{LRU}}^{(\infty)}=\frac{A_{H}}{A_{R}}F(T_{C}). (27)

Proof Sketch: The proof mainly relies on the concentration of the characteristic time established in Theorem C.4 and the Lipschitz continuity of the interarrival CDF FF. For each fixed turn state jj, Theorem C.4 suggests that its hit probability is asymptotically characterized by F⁡(TC)F(T_{C}). However, the characteristic time convergence is not uniform over all turn states. We therefore truncate the reusable-workload series at some level JJ, and compare ∑j=1JSj+1​R¯j​F​(TC)\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j}F(T_{C}) with 𝔼⁡[∑j=1min⁡{M−1,J}Rj​HN,j+1].\mathbb{E}\big[\sum\limits_{j=1}^{\min\{M-1,J\}}R_{j}H_{N,j+1}\big]. For every fixed JJ, the difference between these two quantities vanishes as N→∞N\rightarrow\infty by the characteristic time convergence and the Lipschitz continuity of FF. The remaining contribution from turn states j>Jj>J is controlled by the tail reusable workload ∑j>JSj+1​R¯j\sum_{j>J}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j}, which vanishes as J→∞J\rightarrow\infty. Finally, we conclude Theorem C.5 by first taking N→∞N\rightarrow\infty and then J→∞J\rightarrow\infty. □\square

C.2 Practical MCM Consequence and Theoretically-Motivated Hit Ratio Estimator

In real multi-turn LLM conversation systems, the last KV block generated at each turn is usually partially filled. Therefore, this block does not have a valid hash. We call this block the unhashable tail block. To capture this feature, we introduce a practical multi-turn conversation model (practical MCM). As a modeling approximation, we conservatively assume each completed turn generates one unhashable tail block. Although this block occupies one physical HBM block, it cannot participate in prefix reuse at subsequent turns and can only gradually move toward the LRU end until eviction.

When the conversation proceeds to the next turn, the tokens contained in the unhashable tail block of turn jj must be reprefilled together with the turn-jj response tokens and the turn-(j+1)(j+1) prompt tokens. Accordingly, these tokens can be absorbed into the next turn-wise content increment.

C.2.1 Practical Characteristic Time and Hit Ratio with Unhashable Tail Blocks

We keep the definitions of RjR_{j} and BB as the KV block counts, including the unhashable tail blocks. Hence, the total number of newly generated physical KV blocks is unchanged from the original MCM. The only modification is that, when a conversation is revisited after turn jj, the unhashable tail block cannot participate in prefix reuse, so only Rj−1R_{j}-1 history blocks are hashable and are moved back to the MRU side. We therefore define the expected reusable hashable workload as

AHhash:=∑j≥1Sj+1​𝔼​[Rj−1]=AH−𝔼⁡[M−1].A_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}:=\sum_{j\geq 1}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}[R_{j}-1]=A_{H}-\mathbb{E}[M-1]. (28)

Let DNprac​(t)D_{N}^{\mathrm{prac}}(t) denote the displacement process in the practical system. Because every newly generated physical KV block still contributes to displacement, the new-block contribution remains unchanged. In contrast, each revisit moves one fewer pre-existing history block because the unhashable tail block cannot participate in prefix reuse. Thus, we define the practical mean displacement curve as

dprac​(t):=λ0​𝔼​[B]​t+λ0​AHhash​∫0tF¯​(u)​𝑑u.d_{\mathrm{prac}}(t):=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]t+\lambda_{0}A_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}\int_{0}^{t}\bar{F}(u)du. (29)

Because dprac​(0)=0d_{\mathrm{prac}}(0)=0, limt↑∞dprac​(t)=∞\lim\limits_{t\uparrow\infty}d_{\mathrm{prac}}(t)=\infty, and

dprac′​(t)=λ0​𝔼​[B]+λ0​AHhash​F¯​(t)>0,d_{\mathrm{prac}}^{\prime}(t)=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]+\lambda_{0}A_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}\bar{F}(t)>0,

there exists a unique practical mean-field characteristic time TCpracT_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}} satisfying

dprac​(TCprac)=1.d_{\mathrm{prac}}(T_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}})=1. (30)

For a turn-jj tagged conversation, let τC,prac(N)​(j)\tau_{C,\mathrm{prac}}^{(N)}(j) denote the HBM residence time of its hashable history content with size Rj−1R_{j}-1, in the absence of a next-turn access.

Finally, we define the practical finite-NN hit ratio as

hprac(N):=𝔼⁡[∑j=1M−1(Rj−1)​HN,j+1prac]AR,h_{\mathrm{prac}}^{(N)}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}(R_{j}-1)H_{N,j+1}^{\mathrm{prac}}\right]}{A_{R}}, (31)

where HN,j+1pracH_{N,j+1}^{\mathrm{prac}} is the indicator of the event that the hashable history content after turn jj remains resident in HBM when the turn-(j+1)(j+1) prompt arrives. The corresponding mean-field limiting hit ratio is defined as

hprac(∞):=AHhashAR​F​(TCprac).h_{\mathrm{prac}}^{(\infty)}:=\frac{A_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}}{A_{R}}F(T_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}}). (32)

We next state the main mean-field convergence result for the practical MCM-LRU system.

Theorem C.6 (Practical Hit Ratio Convergence).

Fix a finite JJ such that SJ+1>0S_{J+1}>0 and T>TCpracT>T_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}}. For every 0<ε<min⁡{TCprac,T−TCprac},0<\varepsilon<\min\{T_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}},T-T_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}}\}, the difference between the practical finite-size hit ratio and the mean-field limiting hit ratio can be bounded, such that

|hprac(N)−hprac(∞)|≤LF​ε​AH,hash(J)AR+KJ,hashAR​pN,Jprac​(ε)+2​𝔼​[B2​eθ​B]​e−θ⁡(J+2)AR,\left|h_{\mathrm{prac}}^{(N)}-h_{\mathrm{prac}}^{(\infty)}\right|\leq\frac{L_{F}\varepsilon A_{H,\mathrm{hash}}^{(J)}}{A_{R}}+\frac{K_{J,\mathrm{hash}}}{A_{R}}\sqrt{p_{N,J}^{\mathrm{prac}}(\varepsilon)}+\frac{2\mathbb{E}[B^{2}e^{\theta B}]e^{-\theta(J+2)}}{A_{R}}, (33)

where LFL_{F} is the Lipschitz constant of FF, pN,Jprac​(ε):=18​VTpracN​mprac2​ε2+𝔼⁡[eθ​B]SJ​exp⁡(−θ​mprac3​N​ε)p_{N,J}^{\mathrm{prac}}(\varepsilon):=\frac{18V_{T}^{\mathrm{prac}}}{Nm_{\mathrm{prac}}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta B}]}{S_{J}}\exp\left(-\frac{\theta m_{\mathrm{prac}}}{3}N\varepsilon\right), and KJ,hash:=∑j=1JSj+1​𝔼⁡[(Rj−1)2]K_{J,\mathrm{hash}}:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(R_{j}-1)^{2}]}. Consequently,

hprac(N)→hprac(∞)=AHhashAR​F​(TCprac).h_{\mathrm{prac}}^{(N)}\rightarrow h_{\mathrm{prac}}^{(\infty)}=\frac{A_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}}{A_{R}}F(T_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}}). (34)

The proof of Theorem C.6 is deferred to Section D.4. It follows the same sequence as in the original MCM-LRU analysis, from displacement-process convergence, via characteristic time convergence, to hit-ratio convergence, which is the same as the map of proofs of Theorems C.2, C.4 and C.5.

C.2.2 Theoretically-Motivated Hit Ratio Estimator

Inspired by the mean-field convergence results in Theorem C.6, we develop a theoretically-motivated estimator for practical LLM inference systems.

Suppose that the empirical workload contains LL conversations. For conversation ii, let MiM_{i} denote its number of turns, Ri,jR_{i,j} the physical history content size after turn jj, and Bi:=Ri,MiB_{i}:=R_{i,M_{i}} its total lifetime KV block count. We define the empirical mean cumulative history content workload as

A^R:=1L​∑i=1L∑j=1MiRi,j,\widehat{A}_{R}:=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\sum_{j=1}^{M_{i}}R_{i,j}, (35)

and the empirical mean hashable workload as

A^Hhash:=1L​∑i=1L∑j=1Mi−1(Ri,j−1).\widehat{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}:=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\sum_{j=1}^{M_{i}-1}(R_{i,j}-1). (36)

The empirical mean total lifetime KV block count and the empirical mean number of turns are defined, respectively, as

𝔼⁡[B]^:=1L​∑i=1LBi,and𝔼⁡[M]^:=1L​∑i=1LMi.\widehat{\mathbb{E}[B]}:=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}B_{i},\quad\text{and}\quad\widehat{\mathbb{E}[M]}:=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}M_{i}. (37)

Let F^\widehat{F} denote the empirical CDF of the prompt interarrival time, and let F¯^​(t):=1−F^​(t)\widehat{\bar{F}}(t):=1-\widehat{F}(t) denote its tail. The practical mean-field characteristic time estimator T^Cprac\widehat{T}_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}} is defined as the unique positive solution to the equation

λ0​𝔼⁡[B]^​T^Cprac+λ0​A^Hhash​∫0T^CpracF¯^​(u)​𝑑u=N.\lambda_{0}\widehat{\mathbb{E}[B]}\widehat{T}_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}}+\lambda_{0}\widehat{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}\int_{0}^{\widehat{T}_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}}}\widehat{\bar{F}}(u)\,du=N. (38)

The corresponding mean-field estimator of the practical hit ratio is

h^pracMF:=A^HhashA^R​F^​(T^Cprac).\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{prac}}^{\mathrm{MF}}:=\frac{\widehat{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}}{\widehat{A}_{R}}\widehat{F}\left(\widehat{T}_{C}^{\mathrm{prac}}\right). (39)

In practice, the complete conversation-level workload trace may not be fully available or predictable. Nonetheless, our estimator does not require direct access to every individual conversation, as long as reasonable prior or externally estimated values of the required workload statistics and the prompt interarrival distribution are available. Specifically, we can substitute the estimates of 𝔼⁡[B]\mathbb{E}[B], ARA_{R}, AHhashA_{H}^{\mathrm{hash}}, and FF into the same mean-field formulas. Therefore, this theoretically-motivated hit ratio estimator remains applicable when partial workload distribution and system dynamics information is available.

Appendix D Proofs

In this section, we provide the proofs of our main results in Appendix C. Our main MCM-LRU mean-field result, the normalized tagged-jj conversation displacement process convergence (Theorem C.2), the tagged-jj characteristic time convergence (Theorem C.4), and the hit ratio convergence (Theorem C.5), are demonstrated in Sections D.1, D.2 and D.3, respectively.

The proof of Theorem C.6 follows essentially the same arguments as those developed for the MCM-LRU system. We will demonstrate it in Section D.4.

D.1 Proof of Theorem C.2

We begin by demonstrating the sample-path convergence of the tagged-conversation displacement process. The proof proceeds in three steps. In Section D.1.1, we first establish a Poisson random measure representation of the displacement process and show in Lemma D.1, that DN,j​(⋅)=ℒDN​(⋅)D_{N,j}(\cdot)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{L}}}{{=}}D_{N}(\cdot) for every turn state jj. In Section D.1.2, we decompose the displacement into two subprocesses: the pre-existing history content contribution and the newly generated KV block contribution. Their respective mean curves are derived in Lemmas D.2 and D.3 respectively, which sum to the mean displacement curve d⁡(t)d(t) in Lemma D.4. Finally, in Section D.1.3, we prove Theorem C.2, by combining the results in Lemmas D.1 and D.4.

D.1.1 Poisson Random Measure Representation of the Displacement Process

We first establish a Poisson random measure representation of the tagged-conversation displacement process in Lemma D.1. Using this Poisson random measure representation, we are prepared to then analyze its mean curve, and finally show the sample path convergence of our normalized displacement process.

Lemma D.1 (Poisson Random Measure Representation of the Displacement Process).

Fix a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty. Recall Assumption B.4, where {Wj}j≥1\{W_{j}\}_{j\geq 1} are i.i.d. interarrival times with cumulative distribution function FF and finite mean μW:=𝔼⁡[W1]\mu_{W}:=\mathbb{E}[W_{1}], independent of the conversation mark (M,{Xj,Yj}j≥1)(M,\{X_{j},Y_{j}\}_{j\geq 1}). Then, for every fixed tagged turn state jj with Sj>0S_{j}>0, the displacement process {DN,j​(t):0≤t≤T}\{D_{N,j}(t):0\leq t\leq T\} admits the representation

DN,j​(t)=ℒDN​(t):=∫𝒵Φt​(z)​𝒩N​(𝑑z),0≤t≤T,D_{N,j}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{L}}}{{=}}D_{N}(t):=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\Phi_{t}(z)\,\mathcal{N}_{N}(dz),\qquad 0\leq t\leq T, (40)

where 𝒩N\mathcal{N}_{N} is a Poisson random measure on the marked conversation trajectory space 𝒵\mathcal{Z} with intensity measure N​νN\nu. The path functional Φt​(z)\Phi_{t}(z) denotes the cumulative KV block mass contributed by the background conversation zz to the displacement process during (0,t](0,t].

For a marked conversation z=(a,ζ)z=(a,\zeta), where aa denote its arrival time and ζ\zeta denote its mark, we define its lifetime span L⁡(ζ):=∑ℓ=1M−1Wℓ,L(\zeta):=\sum_{\ell=1}^{M-1}W_{\ell}, and the envelope

GT(a,ζ):=B(ζ)𝟙{−L(ζ)<a≤T}.G_{T}(a,\zeta):=B(\zeta)\mathds{1}\{-L(\zeta)<a\leq T\}.

Then, for every z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z},

0≤Φs​(z)≤Φt​(z)≤GT​(z),0≤s≤t≤T.0\leq\Phi_{s}(z)\leq\Phi_{t}(z)\leq G_{T}(z),\qquad 0\leq s\leq t\leq T. (41)

Moreover,

VT:=∫𝒵GT​(z)2​ν​(𝑑z)=λ0​T​𝔼​[B2]+λ0​μW​𝔼​[(M−1)​B2]<∞.V_{T}:=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}G_{T}(z)^{2}\,\nu(dz)=\lambda_{0}T\mathbb{E}[B^{2}]+\lambda_{0}\mu_{W}\mathbb{E}[(M-1)B^{2}]<\infty. (42)
Proof.

We first construct the conversation arrivals on the entire time axis ℝ\mathbb{R}, which is a Poisson process with rate N​λ0N\lambda_{0}. Each arrival at time a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} is independently assigned a mark

ζ=(M,{Xℓ,Yℓ}ℓ≥1,{Wℓ}ℓ≥1)∈ℳ,\zeta=\left(M,\{X_{\ell},Y_{\ell}\}_{\ell\geq 1},\{W_{\ell}\}_{\ell\geq 1}\right)\in\mathcal{M},

which specifies the complete trajectory of the corresponding conversation in the mark space ℳ\mathcal{M}. We then let PζP_{\zeta} denote the distribution of the conversation mark ζ\zeta, and let z=(a,ζ)z=(a,\zeta) additionally record the conversation arrival time. The collection of marked conversation trajectories then forms a Poisson random measure 𝒩N\mathcal{N}_{N} on 𝒵:=ℝ×ℳ\mathcal{Z}:=\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{M}, with intensity measure

N​ν​(d​z)=N​λ0​d​a​Pζ​(d​ζ).N\nu(dz)=N\lambda_{0}\,da\,P_{\zeta}(d\zeta).

For a marked background conversation z=(a,ζ)z=(a,\zeta), we let Φt​(z)\Phi_{t}(z) denote the total KV block mass contributed by this conversation that moves ahead of the tagged content during (0,t](0,t]. Under the Palm construction for the tagged conversation, Slivnyak’s theorem (see, e.g., Theorem 1.4.5 in Baccelli and Błaszczyszyn [2010]) implies that, after removing the tagged conversation, the remaining marked background conversation trajectories have the same law as the original stationary marked Poisson process. Moreover, the trajectory of the tagged conversation is independent of the background process. Because the background marked Poisson process is stationary, the displacement process observed from the tagged turn-jj access at time t=0t=0 has the same law for every fixed jj with Sj>0S_{j}>0.

If a background conversation is already active at time 00, then at its next prompt access, its pre-existing history content crosses in front of the tagged content. After this access, those existing blocks remain ahead of the tagged content, so subsequent accesses contribute only newly generated blocks. If a background conversation arrives after time 00, all of its blocks generated by time tt contribute in the same manner. Hence every KV block of a background conversation contributes to displacement at most once.

For a conversation mark ζ\zeta, define its lifetime span by L⁡(ζ):=∑ℓ=1M−1Wℓ.L(\zeta):=\sum_{\ell=1}^{M-1}W_{\ell}. A background conversation can contribute to the displacement over the horizon [0,T][0,T] only if its arrival time aa satisfies a≤Ta\leq T and a+L⁡(ζ)>0a+L(\zeta)>0, or equivalently, −L⁡(ζ)<a≤T-L(\zeta)<a\leq T. Therefore, for every z=(a,ζ)∈𝒵z=(a,\zeta)\in\mathcal{Z}, the path Φ⋅​(z)\Phi_{\cdot}(z) is nondecreasing and satisfies that

0≤Φs(z)≤Φt(z)≤B(ζ)𝟙{−L(ζ)<a≤T}=GT(z),0≤s≤t≤T.0\leq\Phi_{s}(z)\leq\Phi_{t}(z)\leq B(\zeta)\mathds{1}\{-L(\zeta)<a\leq T\}=G_{T}(z),\qquad 0\leq s\leq t\leq T.

We then sum the contributions over all background conversations, and have that

DN​(t)=∫𝒵Φt​(z)​𝒩N​(𝑑z),0≤t≤T.D_{N}(t)=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\Phi_{t}(z)\,\mathcal{N}_{N}(dz),\qquad 0\leq t\leq T.

We next verify the square-integrability of the envelope GTG_{T}. For each fixed mark ζ\zeta, the set of arrival times aa for which GT​(a,ζ)G_{T}(a,\zeta) is nonzero has Lebesgue measure T+L⁡(ζ)T+L(\zeta). Therefore,

VT\displaystyle V_{T} =∫𝒵GT​(z)2​ν​(𝑑z)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}G_{T}(z)^{2}\,\nu(dz)
=λ0​𝔼​[B2​(T+L)]\displaystyle=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}\left[B^{2}(T+L)\right]
=λ0​T​𝔼​[B2]+λ0​μW​𝔼​[(M−1)​B2],\displaystyle=\lambda_{0}T\mathbb{E}[B^{2}]+\lambda_{0}\mu_{W}\mathbb{E}[(M-1)B^{2}],

where we obtain the last equality because the interarrival times are i.i.d. with mean μW\mu_{W} and are independent of (M,{Xℓ,Yℓ}ℓ≥1)(M,\{X_{\ell},Y_{\ell}\}_{\ell\geq 1}). In addition, by Assumption B.3, the finiteness of BB’s M.G.F. around 00 implies that all polynomial moments of BB are finite. Moreover, because every turn contributes at least one KV block, we have M≤BM\leq B almost surely. Hence,

𝔼⁡[(M−1)​B2]≤𝔼⁡[B3]<∞,\mathbb{E}[(M-1)B^{2}]\leq\mathbb{E}[B^{3}]<\infty,

and we conclude (42) because

VT=λ0​T​𝔼​[B2]+λ0​μW​𝔼​[(M−1)​B2]<∞.V_{T}=\lambda_{0}T\mathbb{E}[B^{2}]+\lambda_{0}\mu_{W}\mathbb{E}[(M-1)B^{2}]<\infty.

Finally, because the path functional Φt​(z)\Phi_{t}(z) depends only on the background conversation trajectory and not on the tagged turn state jj, the resulting displacement process has the same law for every fixed jj with Sj>0S_{j}>0. Hence,

DN,j​(⋅)=ℒDN​(⋅),D_{N,j}(\cdot)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{L}}}{{=}}D_{N}(\cdot),

which completes the proof. ∎

D.1.2 Displacement Process Decomposition and the Mean Displacement Curve

Fix a turn index jj with Sj>0S_{j}>0. Under the stationary Palm distribution, suppose that a tagged conversation is accessed at its turn jj at time 00 and moved to the MRU end. Recall that DN,j​(t)D_{N,j}(t) denotes the corresponding displacement process and that, by Lemma D.1,

DN,j​(⋅)=ℒDN​(⋅),D_{N,j}(\cdot)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{L}}}{{=}}D_{N}(\cdot),

where the law of DN​(⋅)D_{N}(\cdot) is independent of the tagged turn state jj.

We now decompose the representative displacement process DN​(t)D_{N}(t) into two subprocesses, similarly to the proof of Lemma D.1:

DN​(t)=DNinit​(t)+DNnew​(t).D_{N}(t)=D_{N}^{\mathrm{init}}(t)+D_{N}^{\mathrm{new}}(t). (43)

Here, DNinit​(t)D_{N}^{\mathrm{init}}(t) denotes the displacement contributed by pre-existing history blocks of background conversations that are already active at time 00 and are moved ahead of the tagged content during the time period (0,t](0,t], during which their subsequent access happens. Additionally, DNnew​(t)D_{N}^{\mathrm{new}}(t) denotes the displacement contributed by newly generated KV blocks during (0,t](0,t].

We first characterize the mean curve of the normalized pre-existing history contribution DNinit​(t)N\frac{D_{N}^{\mathrm{init}}(t)}{N}.

Lemma D.2 (Mean Normalized Initial-Prefix Contribution).

During the time period (0,t](0,t], the total pre-existing history content mass contributed to the displacement process, DNinit​(t)D_{N}^{\mathrm{init}}(t), has the following normalized mean

1N​𝔼​[DNinit​(t)]=λ0​AH​∫0tF¯​(s)​𝑑s,\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}[D_{N}^{\mathrm{init}}(t)]=\lambda_{0}A_{H}\int_{0}^{t}\bar{F}(s)\,ds, (44)

where F¯​(t):=1−F​(t)\bar{F}(t):=1-F(t) denotes the tail probability of the prompt interarrival distribution and AH:=∑j≥1Sj+1​R¯jA_{H}:=\sum_{j\geq 1}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j} denotes the expected amount of reusable history content, as defined in (10).

Proof.

Fix a turn state ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. A conversation that reaches turn ℓ+1\ell+1 has a waiting interval of length WℓW_{\ell} after completing turn ℓ\ell.

Let s<0s<0 denote the time at which this conversation completes turn ℓ\ell, and let its inter-turn waiting time be Wℓ=wW_{\ell}=w. Then its waiting interval is [s,s+w)[s,s+w). For its pre-existing history content to contribute to the displacement during (0,t](0,t], the conversation’s next prompt must arrive no later than time tt. Equivalently, we require

s<0<s+w≤t.s<0<s+w\leq t.

For a fixed ww, the set of waiting times ss satisfying this condition is

−w<s≤min⁡{0,t−w},-w<s\leq\min\{0,t-w\},

the admissible length of which is min⁡{t,w}\min\{t,w\}. Therefore, when we integrate over the stationary time shifts of the marked conversation trajectories, the contribution associated with an inter-turn interval of length ww is weighted by min⁡{t,w}\min\{t,w\}.

To determine how frequently such waiting intervals occur on the stationary time axis, we recall that conversations arrive according to a Poisson process with rate N​λ0N\lambda_{0}. Among these conversations, a fraction Sℓ+1=ℙ⁡(M≥ℓ+1)S_{\ell+1}=\mathbb{P}(M\geq\ell+1) reaches turn ℓ+1\ell+1. In addition, the push-forward time ∑j=1ℓWj\sum\limits_{j=1}^{\ell}W_{j} for each conversation is i.i.d.. Therefore, by the mapping theorem of Poisson process, the arrival process of active turn-ℓ\ell conversations that can reach turn ℓ+1\ell+1 is a Poisson process with rate N​λ0​Sℓ​pℓ=N​λ0​Sℓ+1N\lambda_{0}S_{\ell}p_{\ell}=N\lambda_{0}S_{\ell+1}.

Therefore, by Campbell’s theorem, we obtain the expected number of turn-ℓ\ell waiting intervals that are active at time 00 and terminate during (0,t](0,t]:

𝔼⁡[∫−Wℓmin⁡{0,t−Wℓ}N​λ0​Sℓ+1​𝑑s]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{-W_{\ell}}^{\min\{0,t-W_{\ell}\}}N\lambda_{0}S_{\ell+1}ds\bigg] =N​λ0​Sℓ+1​𝔼​[min⁡{t,Wℓ}]\displaystyle=N\lambda_{0}S_{\ell+1}\mathbb{E}[\min\{t,W_{\ell}\}]
=N​λ0​Sℓ+1​∫0tℙ⁡(Wℓ>u)​𝑑u\displaystyle=N\lambda_{0}S_{\ell+1}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{P}(W_{\ell}>u)\,du
=N​λ0​Sℓ+1​∫0tF¯​(u)​𝑑u.\displaystyle=N\lambda_{0}S_{\ell+1}\int_{0}^{t}\bar{F}(u)\,du.

At the terminating prompt of each such interval, its pre-existing history content of size RℓR_{\ell} is moved in front of the tagged content. Because WℓW_{\ell} is independent of the conversation length and block increments, the expected turn-ℓ\ell history contribution is therefore

N​λ0​Sℓ+1​R¯ℓ​∫0tF¯​(u)​𝑑u.N\lambda_{0}S_{\ell+1}\bar{R}_{\ell}\int_{0}^{t}\bar{F}(u)\,du.

Summing over all ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 and recalling that AH=∑ℓ≥1Sℓ+1​R¯ℓA_{H}=\sum_{\ell\geq 1}S_{\ell+1}\bar{R}_{\ell}, we obtain that

𝔼⁡[DNinit​(t)]=N​λ0​AH​∫0tF¯​(u)​𝑑u.\mathbb{E}[D_{N}^{\mathrm{init}}(t)]=N\lambda_{0}A_{H}\int_{0}^{t}\bar{F}(u)\,du.

∎

Similarly, the normalized new blocks contribution DNnew​(t)N\frac{D_{N}^{\mathrm{new}}(t)}{N} admits the following expectation, where we recall from (4) and (5) that B:=RMB:=R_{M} denotes the total lifetime KV block numbers of a conversation.

Lemma D.3 (Mean Normalized New Blocks Contribution).

For every t≥0t\geq 0, we let DNnew​(t)D_{N}^{\mathrm{new}}(t) denote the new blocks generated by new prompts in the time duration (0,t](0,t]. Then the mean of this normalized contribution is

1N​𝔼​[DNnew​(t)]=λ0​𝔼​[B]​t.\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}[D_{N}^{\mathrm{new}}(t)]=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]t. (45)
Proof.

In stationarity, an active conversation at turn state jj generates a new prompt, with mean number of blocks 𝔼⁡[Zj+1]=𝔼⁡[Xj+1+Yj]\mathbb{E}[Z_{j+1}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{j+1}+Y_{j}]. In addition, recall our argument in the proof of Lemma D.2, that the arrival of these turn-(j+1)(j+1) prompts forms a Poisson process with rate N​λ0​Sj+1N\lambda_{0}S_{j+1}. In addition, the new conversation has arrival rate N​λ0N\lambda_{0}, each contributes blocks with mean 𝔼⁡[Z1]=𝔼​X1\mathbb{E}[Z_{1}]=\mathbb{E}X_{1}. Therefore, the total new block growth rate due to new block arrivals is

∑j≥1N​λ0​Sj​𝔼​[Zj]=∑j≥1N​λ0​Sj+1​𝔼​[Xj+1+Yj]+N​λ0​𝔼​[X1]\sum\limits_{j\geq 1}N\lambda_{0}S_{j}\mathbb{E}[Z_{j}]=\sum\limits_{j\geq 1}N\lambda_{0}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}[X_{j+1}+Y_{j}]+N\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[X_{1}] (46)

Because B=RMB=R_{M}, by Assumption B.2, we have that

𝔼⁡[B]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[B] =𝔼⁡[X1]+𝔼⁡[∑j=1M−1Xj+1+Yj]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]+\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum\limits_{j=1}^{M-1}X_{j+1}+Y_{j}\Big]
=𝔼[X1]+∑j≥1𝔼[(Xj+1+Yj)𝟙{M≥j+1}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]+\sum_{j\geq 1}\mathbb{E}[(X_{j+1}+Y_{j})\mathds{1}\{M\geq j+1\}]
=𝔼⁡[X1]+∑j≥1Sj+1​𝔼​[Xj+1+Yj].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]+\sum_{j\geq 1}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}[X_{j+1}+Y_{j}].

Therefore, we conclude (45). ∎

Now we combine Lemmas D.2 and D.3 to obtain the following mean displacement curve.

Lemma D.4 (Mean Displacement Curve).

For every t≥0t\geq 0, the displacement process DN,j​(t)D_{N,j}(t) has the same law as DN​(t)D_{N}(t) for every fixed tagged turn state jj with Sj>0S_{j}>0. Moreover,

1N​𝔼​[DN​(t)]=d⁡(t):=λ0​𝔼​[B]​t+λ0​AH​∫0tF¯​(s)​𝑑s,\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}[D_{N}(t)]=d(t):=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]t+\lambda_{0}A_{H}\int_{0}^{t}\bar{F}(s)\,ds, (47)

where F¯​(t):=1−F​(t)\bar{F}(t):=1-F(t) denotes the tail probability of FF. Moreover, dd is strictly increasing and Lipschitz-continuous, with

λ0​𝔼​[B]​(t−s)≤d⁡(t)−d⁡(s)≤λ0​(𝔼⁡[B]+AH)​(t−s),for all ​0≤s≤t.\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B](t-s)\leq d(t)-d(s)\leq\lambda_{0}(\mathbb{E}[B]+A_{H})(t-s),\qquad\text{for all }0\leq s\leq t.
Proof.

We obtain (47) by directly combining Lemmas D.2 and D.3.

Because 0≤F¯​(u)≤10\leq\bar{F}(u)\leq 1, for every 0≤s≤t0\leq s\leq t,

d⁡(t)−d⁡(s)=λ0​𝔼​[B]​(t−s)+λ0​AH​∫stF¯​(u)​𝑑u,\displaystyle d(t)-d(s)=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B](t-s)+\lambda_{0}A_{H}\int_{s}^{t}\bar{F}(u)\,du,

and hence

λ0​𝔼​[B]​(t−s)≤d⁡(t)−d⁡(s)≤λ0​(𝔼⁡[B]+AH)​(t−s).\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B](t-s)\leq d(t)-d(s)\leq\lambda_{0}(\mathbb{E}[B]+A_{H})(t-s).

Thus dd is strictly increasing and Lipschitz-continuous. ∎

D.1.3 Sample Path Convergence of the Normalized Displacement Process

We are now prepared to prove Theorem C.2, the finite-size concentration and sample path convergence of the normalized displacement process.

By Lemma D.1, for every fixed turn state jj with Sj>0S_{j}>0, the process {DN,j​(t):0≤t≤T}\{D_{N,j}(t):0\leq t\leq T\} has the same law as the canonical displacement process {DN​(t):0≤t≤T}\{D_{N}(t):0\leq t\leq T\}. We therefore omit the tagged turn-state index jj and study DN​(t)D_{N}(t) directly.

Theorem C.2 (Sample-Path Convergence of the Normalized Displacement Process).

The tagged turn-jj content process follows the same law, such that DN,j​(⋅)​=𝑑​DN​(⋅)D_{N,j}(\cdot)\overset{d}{=}D_{N}(\cdot) for every turn state jj. In addition, for a fixed T<∞T<\infty, let VT=λ0​T​𝔼​[B2]+λ0​μW​𝔼​[(M−1)​B2]<∞.V_{T}=\lambda_{0}T\mathbb{E}[B^{2}]+\lambda_{0}\mu_{W}\mathbb{E}[(M-1)B^{2}]<\infty., and let L:=sup0≤t≤Td′​(t)=λ0​𝔼​[B]+λ0​AHL:=\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}d^{\prime}(t)=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]+\lambda_{0}A_{H}. Then, for every t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and every ε>0\varepsilon>0,

ℙ⁡(|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|>ε)≤VTN​ε2.\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq\frac{V_{T}}{N\varepsilon^{2}}.

Moreover, for every 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1,

ℙ⁡(sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|>ε)≤CTN​ε3,\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq\frac{C_{T}}{N\varepsilon^{3}},

where CT:=16​VT9​(2+4​L​T).C_{T}:=\frac{16V_{T}}{9}(2+4LT).

Consequently, for any fixed T≥0T\geq 0,

sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|→ℙ0.\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0.

In particular, the finite-size bounds imply

|DN​(t)N−d(t)|=Oℙ(N−1/2)\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|=O_{\mathbb{P}}(N^{-1/2})

for every fixed tt, and

sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d(t)|=Oℙ(N−1/3).\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|=O_{\mathbb{P}}(N^{-1/3}).
Proof.

For every t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], the Poisson random measure representation in Lemma D.1 gives that

Var​(DN​(t)N)=1N​∫𝒵Φt2​(z)​ν​(𝑑z)≤1N​∫𝒵GT2​(z)​ν​(𝑑z)=VTN.\text{Var}\left(\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}\right)=\frac{1}{N}\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\Phi_{t}^{2}(z)\,\nu(dz)\leq\frac{1}{N}\int_{\mathcal{Z}}G_{T}^{2}(z)\,\nu(dz)=\frac{V_{T}}{N}. (48)

In addition, due to Lemma D.4, 1N​𝔼​[DN​(t)]=d⁡(t)\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}[D_{N}(t)]=d(t), we have that

sup0≤t≤T𝔼⁡[|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|2]≤VTN.\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{V_{T}}{N}. (49)

Therefore, applying Chebyshev’s inequality, we first derive the following pointwise second-moment bound for any ε>0\varepsilon>0:

ℙ⁡(|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|>ε)≤1ε2​𝔼​[|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|2]≤VTN​ε2.\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{V_{T}}{N\varepsilon^{2}}.

We next demonstrate the upper bound for the sample-path 𝕃∞\mathbb{L}^{\infty}-difference. Recall from Lemma D.4 that for any t>0t>0,

d′​(t)=λ0​𝔼​[B]+λ0​AH​F¯​(t)≤L:=d′​(0)=λ0​𝔼​[B]+λ0​AH.d^{\prime}(t)=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]+\lambda_{0}A_{H}\bar{F}(t)\leq L:=d^{\prime}(0)=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B]+\lambda_{0}A_{H}.

Hence, the mean displacement curve dd is LL-Lipschitz.

Fix 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1. Choose an equal partition

Π={t0,⋯,tK},where0=t0<t1<⋯<tK=T,\Pi=\{t_{0},\cdots,t_{K}\},\quad\text{where}\quad 0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{K}=T,

satisfying that

‖Π‖:=max0≤k<K⁡(tk+1−tk)≤ε4​L.\|\Pi\|:=\max_{0\leq k<K}(t_{k+1}-t_{k})\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{4L}.

It is enough to choose K+1≤2+4​L​TεK+1\leq 2+\frac{4LT}{\varepsilon}, i.e., K=⌊1+4​L​Tε⌋K=\lfloor 1+\frac{4LT}{\varepsilon}\rfloor.

Fix t∈[tk,tk+1]t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}]. Because DN​(t)D_{N}(t) and d⁡(t)d(t) are both nondecreasing,

DN​(tk)≤DN​(t)≤DN​(tk+1)andd⁡(tk)≤d⁡(t)≤d⁡(tk+1).D_{N}(t_{k})\leq D_{N}(t)\leq D_{N}(t_{k+1})\quad\text{and}\quad d(t_{k})\leq d(t)\leq d(t_{k+1}).

Therefore,

DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)\displaystyle\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t) ≤DN​(tk+1)N−d⁡(tk)\displaystyle\leq\frac{D_{N}(t_{k+1})}{N}-d(t_{k})
=(DN​(tk+1)N−d⁡(tk+1))+(d⁡(tk+1)−d⁡(tk))\displaystyle=\left(\frac{D_{N}(t_{k+1})}{N}-d(t_{k+1})\right)+\left(d(t_{k+1})-d(t_{k})\right)
≤|DN​(tk+1)N−d⁡(tk+1)|+ε4.\displaystyle\leq\left|\frac{D_{N}(t_{k+1})}{N}-d(t_{k+1})\right|+\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.

and similarly,

d⁡(t)−DN​(t)N≤|DN​(tk)N−d⁡(tk)|+ε4.d(t)-\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}\leq\left|\frac{D_{N}(t_{k})}{N}-d(t_{k})\right|+\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.

To establish

sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|≤ε,\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|\leq\varepsilon,

it is enough to let, for any 1≤k≤K1\leq k\leq K

max0≤k≤K⁡|DN​(tk)N−d⁡(tk)|≤3​ε4.\max_{0\leq k\leq K}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t_{k})}{N}-d(t_{k})\right|\leq\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}.

Therefore, we can bound the L∞L^{\infty}-distance via a union bound, such that

ℙ⁡(sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|>ε)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|>\varepsilon\right) ≤∑k=0Kℙ⁡(|DN​(tk)N−d⁡(tk)|>3​ε4)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{K}\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{D_{N}(t_{k})}{N}-d(t_{k})\right|>\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\right)
≤(K+1)​16​VT9​N​ε2\displaystyle\leq(K+1)\frac{16V_{T}}{9N\varepsilon^{2}}
≤(2+4​L​Tε)​16​VT9​N​ε2.\displaystyle\leq(2+\frac{4LT}{\varepsilon})\frac{16V_{T}}{9N\varepsilon^{2}}.

When 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1, the last term can be further bounded by

(2+4​L​Tε)​16​VT9​N​ε2≤2+4​L​Tε​16​VT9​N​ε2=CTN​ε3.(2+\frac{4LT}{\varepsilon})\frac{16V_{T}}{9N\varepsilon^{2}}\leq\frac{2+4LT}{\varepsilon}\frac{16V_{T}}{9N\varepsilon^{2}}=\frac{C_{T}}{N\varepsilon^{3}}.

We finally show the convergence result with the given rate. For the pointwise convergence rate, set ε=δ/N\varepsilon=\delta/\sqrt{N} for some fixed δ>0\delta>0 in (16). Then

ℙ⁡(N​|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|>δ)≤VTδ2.\mathbb{P}\left(\sqrt{N}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|>\delta\right)\leq\frac{V_{T}}{\delta^{2}}.

Taking lim supN→∞\limsup_{N\to\infty} and then δ→∞\delta\to\infty, we have that

|DN​(t)N−d(t)|=Oℙ(N−1/2).\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|=O_{\mathbb{P}}(N^{-1/2}).

For the sample-path convergence rate, set ε=δN−1/3\varepsilon=\delta N^{-1/3} in (17). For every fixed δ>0\delta>0 and all sufficiently large NN, ε≤1\varepsilon\leq 1, and

ℙ⁡(N1/3​sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d⁡(t)|>δ)≤CTδ3.\mathbb{P}\left(N^{1/3}\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|>\delta\right)\leq\frac{C_{T}}{\delta^{3}}.

Taking lim supN→∞\limsup_{N\to\infty} and then δ→∞\delta\to\infty, we have that

sup0≤t≤T|DN​(t)N−d(t)|=Oℙ(N−1/3).\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left|\frac{D_{N}(t)}{N}-d(t)\right|=O_{\mathbb{P}}(N^{-1/3}).

Finally, because DN,j​(⋅)=ℒDN​(⋅)D_{N,j}(\cdot)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{L}}}{{=}}D_{N}(\cdot) for every fixed turn state jj with Sj>0S_{j}>0, the same concentration bounds, convergence in probability, and finite-size rates hold for the normalized tagged-conversation displacement process DN,j​(⋅)N\frac{D_{N,j}(\cdot)}{N}. This completes the proof. ∎

D.2 Proof of Theorem C.4

We next focus on proving the convergence of the eviction time of a tagged turn-jj conversation content. First, we bound the tail of the turn-jj conversation content length RjR_{j} for each j≥1j\geq 1, via the following lemma.

Lemma D.5 (Tail Bound of Turn-jj Content Length).

Fix a turn state jj such that Sj>0S_{j}>0. For any fixed θ∈(0,θ0)\theta\in(0,\theta_{0}), we have the following tail bound

ℙ⁡(Rj>x)≤𝔼⁡[eθ​B]Sj​e−θ​x,x≥0.\mathbb{P}(R_{j}>x)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta B}]}{S_{j}}e^{-\theta x},\qquad x\geq 0. (50)

Consequently,

Rj=Oℙ​(1).R_{j}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(1). (51)
Proof.

By Assumption B.2, the block increments are independent of MM. Because RjR_{j} depends only on the block increments up to turn jj, RjR_{j} is independent of MM. Hence,

𝔼⁡[eθ​Rj]=𝔼⁡[eθ​Rj∣M≥j].\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta R_{j}}]=\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta R_{j}}\mid M\geq j].

Conditional on the event {M≥j}\{M\geq j\}, the turn-jj history content is contained in the total lifetime block mass, and therefore Rj≤BR_{j}\leq B. Hence,

𝔼[eθ​Rj]=1Sj𝔼[eθ​Rj𝟙{M≥j}]≤1Sj𝔼[eθ​B𝟙{M≥j}]≤𝔼⁡[eθ​B]Sj.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta R_{j}}]=\frac{1}{S_{j}}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\theta R_{j}}\mathds{1}\{M\geq j\}\right]\leq\frac{1}{S_{j}}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\theta B}\mathds{1}\{M\geq j\}\right]\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta B}]}{S_{j}}.

Applying Markov’s inequality, we obtain the following bound for every x>0x>0:

ℙ⁡(Rj>x)≤e−θ​x​𝔼​[eθ​Rj]≤𝔼⁡[eθ​B]Sj​e−θ​x.\mathbb{P}(R_{j}>x)\leq e^{-\theta x}\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta R_{j}}]\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta B}]}{S_{j}}e^{-\theta x}.

Because the distribution of RjR_{j} is independent of NN, the family {Rj}N≥1\{R_{j}\}_{N\geq 1} is tight, and hence Rj=Oℙ​(1)R_{j}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(1). ∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem C.4.

Theorem C.4 (Characteristic Time Convergence).

Fix a turn state jj such that Sj>0S_{j}>0, and a finite horizon T>TCT>T_{C}. For every

0<ε<min⁡{TC,T−TC},0<\varepsilon<\min\{T_{C},T-T_{C}\},

the characteristic time satisfies

ℙ⁡(|τC(N)​(j)−TC|>ε)≤18​VTN​cd2​ε2+𝔼⁡[eθ​B]Sj​exp⁡(−θ​cd3​N​ε)=pN,j​(ε),\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)-T_{C}\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq\frac{18V_{T}}{Nc_{d}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta B}]}{S_{j}}\exp\left(-\frac{\theta c_{d}}{3}N\varepsilon\right)=p_{N,j}(\varepsilon),

where cd:=λ0​𝔼​[B]c_{d}:=\lambda_{0}\mathbb{E}[B] and VT:=∫𝒵GT​(z)2​ν​(𝑑z)<∞V_{T}:=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}G_{T}(z)^{2}\,\nu(dz)<\infty is the second-moment constant introduced in Lemma D.1. Consequently,

D.3 Proof of Theorem C.5

We finally establish the mean-field convergence of the hit ratio under the whole-content LRU policy. For every j≥2j\geq 2, recall that HN,jH_{N,j} denotes the indicator that the history content of size Rj−1R_{j-1} remains resident in HBM when the turn-jj prompt arrives.

To analyze the limiting behavior of the hit ratio, we first define some auxiliary notations.

Recall that AH=∑j≥1Sj+1​R¯jA_{H}=\sum_{j\geq 1}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j} denotes the expected amount of reusable history content workload. We further define AH(J)A_{H}^{(J)} as a truncation of AHA_{H} at level J≥1J\geq 1, i.e.,

AH(J):=∑j=1JSj+1​R¯j.A_{H}^{(J)}:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j}. (57)

The tail workload is then defined such that

𝒯J:=∑j>JSj+1​R¯j=AH−AH(J).\mathcal{T}_{J}:=\sum_{j>J}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j}=A_{H}-A_{H}^{(J)}. (58)

In addition, we let

KJ:=∑j=1JSj+1​𝔼⁡[Rj2]K_{J}:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[R_{j}^{2}]} (59)

which will be used to control the finite-JJ approximation error.

We prove Theorem C.5 through the following lemmas. We first establish an exact representation of the finite-NN LRU hit ratio in terms of the characteristic time. Recall that WjW_{j}, the prompt interarrival time between turns jj and j+1j+1, has cumulative distribution function FF. By the definition of the characteristic time, we have that

HN,j+1=𝟙{Wj<τC(N)(j)}.H_{N,j+1}=\mathds{1}\left\{W_{j}<\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right\}. (60)
Lemma D.6 (Exact Representation of the LRU Hit Ratio).

For every NN, the hit ratio admits the representation

h(N)=1AR​∑j≥1Sj+1​𝔼​[Rj​F​(τCN​(j))].h^{(N)}=\frac{1}{A_{R}}\sum_{j\geq 1}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}F(\tau^{N}_{C}(j))\right]. (61)
Proof.

By Assumption B.4, the tagged-conversation interarrival time WjW_{j} is independent of the block increments and hence of RjR_{j}. Moreover, the displacement process is determined entirely by the background conversations, which are independent of the tagged conversation. Therefore, WjW_{j} is independent of (Rj,τC(N)​(j))(R_{j},\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)). Conditioning on (Rj,τC(N)​(j))(R_{j},\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)) gives

𝔼[HN,j+1∣Rj,τC(N)(j)]=ℙ(Wj<τC(N)(j)∣Rj,τC(N)(j))=F(τC(N)(j))\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[H_{N,j+1}\mid R_{j},\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right]=\mathbb{P}\left(W_{j}<\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\mid R_{j},\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right)=F\big(\tau^{(N)}_{C}(j)\big)

Using (24),

𝔼[∑j=1M−1RjHN,j+1]=∑j≥1𝔼[RjHN,j+1𝟙{M≥j+1}].\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}R_{j}H_{N,j+1}\right]=\sum_{j\geq 1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}H_{N,j+1}\mathds{1}\{M\geq j+1\}\right].

Additionally, according to Assumption B.2, MM is independent of the block increment. Hence,

𝔼[RjHN,j+1𝟙{M≥j+1}]=Sj+1𝔼[RjHN,j+1]=Sj+1𝔼[RjF(τCN(j))].\mathbb{E}\Big[R_{j}H_{N,j+1}\mathds{1}\{M\geq j+1\}\Big]=S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}H_{N,j+1}\right]=S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}F(\tau^{N}_{C}(j))\right]. (62)

By summing over j≥1j\geq 1 and dividing by ARA_{R}, we prove (61). ∎

Recall in Theorem C.4, that the convergence of τC(N)​(j)\tau^{(N)}_{C}(j) is not uniform in jj. We therefore first use the finite-turn proxy

∑j=1JSj+1​𝔼​[Rj​F​(τCN​(j))].\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}F(\tau^{N}_{C}(j))\right]. (63)

The difference between the finite-size and limiting hit ratios can then be decomposed into two parts: the tail contributions beyond turn JJ, which are controlled by 𝒯J\mathcal{T}_{J}, and the truncated approximation error |∑j=1JSj+1​𝔼​[Rj​F​(τCN​(j))]−AH(J)​F​(TC)|\left|\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}F(\tau^{N}_{C}(j))\right]-A_{H}^{(J)}F(T_{C})\right|, which can be bounded via the following lemma.

Lemma D.7 (Finite-Turn Hit Ratio Error).

Fix a finite JJ such that SJ+1>0S_{J+1}>0. For every 0<ε<min⁡{TC,T−TC}0<\varepsilon<\min\{T_{C},T-T_{C}\},

|∑j=1JSj+1​𝔼​[Rj​F​(τCN​(j))]−AH(J)​F​(TC)|≤LF​ε​AH(J)+KJ​pN,J​(ε).\left|\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}F(\tau^{N}_{C}(j))\right]-A_{H}^{(J)}F(T_{C})\right|\leq L_{F}\varepsilon A_{H}^{(J)}+K_{J}\sqrt{p_{N,J}(\varepsilon)}. (64)
Proof.

By the triangle inequality, the L.H.S. of (64) can be bounded such that

|∑j=1JSj+1​𝔼​[Rj​F​(τC(N)​(j))]−∑j=1JSj+1​R¯j​F​(TC)|≤∑j=1JSj+1​𝔼​[Rj​|F⁡(τC(N)​(j))−F⁡(TC)|],\displaystyle\left|\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}F\left(\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right)\right]-\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j}F(T_{C})\right|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}\left|F\left(\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right)-F(T_{C})\right|\right],

Due to Assumption B.4, F⁡(⋅)F(\cdot) is LFL_{F}-Lipschitz, i.e.,

|F⁡(t)−F⁡(s)|≤LF​|t−s|,for all ​0≤t<s<∞.|F(t)-F(s)|\leq L_{F}|t-s|,\qquad\text{for all }0\leq t<s<\infty.

For every j≤Jj\leq J, we define the concentration event 𝒢N,j(ε):={|τC(N)(j)−TC|≤ε}\mathcal{G}_{N,j}(\varepsilon):=\left\{\left|\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)-T_{C}\right|\leq\varepsilon\right\}. On 𝒢N,j​(ε)\mathcal{G}_{N,j}(\varepsilon), the Lipschitz condition implies that

|F⁡(τC(N)​(j))−F⁡(TC)|≤LF​ε.\left|F\left(\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right)-F(T_{C})\right|\leq L_{F}\varepsilon.

Because 0≤F⁡(t)≤10\leq F(t)\leq 1 for all t≥0t\geq 0, on the complementary event 𝒢N,j​(ε)c\mathcal{G}_{N,j}(\varepsilon)^{c} we still have |F⁡(τC(N)​(j))−F⁡(TC)|≤1\left|F\left(\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right)-F(T_{C})\right|\leq 1. Therefore,

𝔼⁡[Rj​|F⁡(τC(N)​(j))−F⁡(TC)|]≤LF​ε​𝔼​[Rj]+𝔼⁡[Rj​𝟙​{𝒢N,j​(ε)c}].\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}\left|F\left(\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right)-F(T_{C})\right|\right]\leq L_{F}\varepsilon\mathbb{E}[R_{j}]+\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}\mathds{1}\left\{\mathcal{G}_{N,j}(\varepsilon)^{c}\right\}\right].

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

𝔼⁡[Rj​𝟙​{𝒢N,j​(ε)c}]≤𝔼⁡[Rj2]​ℙ⁡(|τC(N)​(j)−TC|>ε).\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}\mathds{1}\left\{\mathcal{G}_{N,j}(\varepsilon)^{c}\right\}\right]\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[R_{j}^{2}]}\sqrt{\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)-T_{C}\right|>\varepsilon\right)}.

According to Theorem C.4,

ℙ⁡(|τC(N)​(j)−TC|>ε)≤pN,j​(ε).\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)-T_{C}\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq p_{N,j}(\varepsilon).

Moreover, because SjS_{j} is nonincreasing in jj, we have Sj≥SJS_{j}\geq S_{J} for every j≤Jj\leq J. Hence, the finite-size bound in Theorem C.4 implies pN,j​(ε)≤pN,J​(ε),p_{N,j}(\varepsilon)\leq p_{N,J}(\varepsilon), and therefore

ℙ⁡(|τC(N)​(j)−TC|>ε)≤pN,J​(ε).\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)-T_{C}\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq p_{N,J}(\varepsilon).

It follows that for each 1≤j≤J1\leq j\leq J,

𝔼⁡[Rj​|F⁡(τC(N)​(j))−F⁡(TC)|]≤LF​ε​R¯j+𝔼⁡[Rj2]​pN,J​(ε).\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}\left|F\left(\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right)-F(T_{C})\right|\right]\leq L_{F}\varepsilon\bar{R}_{j}+\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[R_{j}^{2}]}\sqrt{p_{N,J}(\varepsilon)}.

Multiplying by Sj+1S_{j+1} and summing over j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,J, we obtain that

∑j=1JSj+1​𝔼​[Rj​|F⁡(τC(N)​(j))−F⁡(TC)|]≤LF​ε​AH(J)+KJ​pN,J​(ε),\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}\left|F\left(\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right)-F(T_{C})\right|\right]\leq L_{F}\varepsilon A_{H}^{(J)}+K_{J}\sqrt{p_{N,J}(\varepsilon)},

and we prove (64). ∎

We next control the error of the tail workload 𝒯J=∑j>JSj+1​R¯j\mathcal{T}_{J}=\sum\limits_{j>J}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j}, via the lemma below.

Lemma D.8 (Bound for the Tail Workload).

For every integer J≥1J\geq 1 and any fixed θ∈(0,θ0)\theta\in(0,\theta_{0}), the tail workload 𝒯J\mathcal{T}_{J} has the following upper bound:

𝒯J≤𝔼⁡[B2​eθ​B]​e−θ⁡(J+2).\mathcal{T}_{J}\leq\mathbb{E}[B^{2}e^{\theta B}]e^{-\theta(J+2)}. (65)

𝒯J→0.\mathcal{T}_{J}\rightarrow 0. (66)

x Using the independence between MM and the block increments RjR_{j}’s, we can rewrite 𝒯J\mathcal{T}_{J}, such that

𝒯J=∑j>JSj+1R¯j=∑j>J𝔼[Rj𝟙{M≥j+1}]=𝔼[∑j=J+1M−1Rj].\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{J}=\sum_{j>J}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j}=\sum_{j>J}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}\mathds{1}\{M\geq j+1\}\right]=\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{j=J+1}^{M-1}R_{j}\Big].

For any fixed θ∈(0,θ0)\theta\in(0,\theta_{0}), because 𝟙{B≥J+2}≤eθ⁡(B−J−2)\mathds{1}\{B\geq J+2\}\leq e^{\theta(B-J-2)},

B2𝟙{B≥J+2}≤B2eθ​Be−θ⁡(J+2)⇒𝒯J≤𝔼[B2eθ​B]e−θ⁡(J+2),B^{2}\mathds{1}\{B\geq J+2\}\leq B^{2}e^{\theta B}e^{-\theta(J+2)}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathcal{T}_{J}\leq\mathbb{E}[B^{2}e^{\theta B}]e^{-\theta(J+2)},

and we conclude Lemma D.8. ∎

+1AR∑j>JSj+1𝔼[RjF(τC(N)(j))]+1AR∑j>JSj+1R¯jF(TC).\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{A_{R}}\sum_{j>J}S_{j+1}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{j}F\left(\tau_{C}^{(N)}(j)\right)\right]+\frac{1}{A_{R}}\sum_{j>J}S_{j+1}\bar{R}_{j}F(T_{C}).

Appendix E Theoretically-Motivated Estimator and LLM Serving Experiments

In this section, we provide a more detailed explanation of the settings and the result analysis, of our empirical LLM serving experiments in Section 4.

Our experiments run Qwen3-8B on five Ascend 910B2 NPUs using a Prefill-Decode disaggregation architecture, with one NPU as the prefiller and four as the decoder pool. Each NPU provides approximately 64 GB of HBM, and the model is deployed under BF16 precision. We reserve 40 GB of the prefiller HBM exclusively for KV cache. With 36 transformer layers, 8 KV heads per layer, and a head dimension of 128, Qwen3-8B requires

KV Bytes/token=2×36×8×128×2=144​ KB,\text{KV Bytes/token}=2\times 36\times 8\times 128\times 2=144\text{ KB},

where the leading factor 22 corresponds to the Key (K) and Value (V) matrices. With a block size of 128 tokens, each KV block occupies 18 MB, and an HBM capacity of N=⌊40​ GB/18​ MB⌋=2,275N=\lfloor 40\text{ GB}/18\text{ MB}\rfloor=2{,}275 blocks. Our software stack consists of vLLM v0.22.1, vLLM-Ascend v0.22.1rc1, and Mooncake v0.3.9 for KV transfer between the prefill and decode pools.

As mentioned in Section 4, we construct the workload from the public ShareGPT dataset (ShareGPT [2026]) and sample 6,000 conversations containing at least two turns. The first 1,000 conversations with 4,690 turns are used for cache warm-up and are sufficient to fill the HBM before measurement. The remaining 5,000 conversations form the measurement set. Conversation submissions in both phases follow Poisson processes with some rates specified below. The measurement window starts at the submission time t1t_{1} of the first conversation in the measurement set and ends at the submission time t5000t_{5000} of the last. This finite horizon may censor some late turns of active conversations, but we avoid increasing the hit ratio by continuing measurement after new conversation arrivals have stopped.

All block-level workload statistics are computed using the Qwen3 tokenizer and chat template. Fig. 2 shows the empirical conversation-turn distribution and the marginal distribution of new KV blocks per turn. We note that our estimator does not require block increments to be i.i.d. across turns. Using the formulas in equations (35) to (37), we have that

A^R=38.9092,A^Hhash=22.5178,𝔼​B^=12.9220,and𝔼​M^=4.4694.\hat{A}_{R}=38.9092,\quad\hat{A}_{H}^{\text{hash}}=22.5178,\quad\widehat{\mathbb{E}B}=12.9220,\quad\text{and}\quad\widehat{\mathbb{E}M}=4.4694.

Because ShareGPT provides both prompts and recorded responses, we replay the original conversation text rather than sending generated responses into subsequent turns. For each turn, the decoder is forced to generate the same number of tokens as the corresponding recorded response, preserving the decoding workload and timing, but the generated text and its response KV cache are discarded. This prevents inconsistencies between generated responses and subsequent recorded prompts while preserving the empirical KV-cache workload evolution.

In our experiment, we use the LRU policy equipped in vLLM, which has the following differences from our theoretical model:

  1. 1.

    A block’s effective recency timestamp is not the arrival time of its latest prompt. Instead, it is determined by system events including completion of prefill-to-decode KV transfer, CPU DRAM write-back, and prefill accesses.

  2. 2.

    Blocks with nonzero reference counts are temporarily protected from eviction, even if they are currently the LRU blocks.

  3. 3.

    Blocks belonging to the same conversation do not share identical timestamps. In particular, vLLM exhibits a prefix-preserving, suffix-first eviction behavior, so the cache boundary may partially evict a conversation suffix rather than the entire conversation cohort.

  4. 4.

    Different conversations may share identical prefix blocks, e.g., through a common system prompt. However, in our experiment, such a cross-conversation prefix sharing is negligible ShareGPT workload used in our experiment.

In Experiment 1, we fix the conversation arrival rate at λ0=1.5\lambda_{0}=1.5 and vary the target mean prompt interarrival time μF\mu_{F}. For turn jj of conversation ii, we let Wi​jE2EW_{ij}^{\mathrm{E2E}} denote the end-to-end (E2E) time required to complete decoding, and we independently sample Wi​jsample∼Exp​(1/μF)W_{ij}^{\mathrm{sample}}\sim\text{Exp}(1/\mu_{F}). Because the next prompt cannot be submitted before the preceding response is completed, the realized interarrival time is

Wi​j=max⁡{Wi​jE2E,Wi​jsample}.W_{ij}=\max\{W_{ij}^{\mathrm{E2E}},W_{ij}^{\mathrm{sample}}\}. (80)

The prior estimator uses the target exponential CDF F(t)=1−exp(−t/μF)F(t)=1-\exp(-t/\mu_{F}). After each experiment, we compute the empirical mean interarrival time μ^F\hat{\mu}_{F} and use the posterior CDF Fpost(t)=1−exp(−t/μ^F)F^{\mathrm{post}}(t)=1-\exp(-t/\hat{\mu}_{F}). We report the absolute error AE=|estimated hit ratio−actual hit ratio|\mathrm{AE}=|\text{estimated hit ratio}-\text{actual hit ratio}| and relative error RE=AE/actual hit ratio×100%\mathrm{RE}=\mathrm{AE}/\text{actual hit ratio}\times 100\%.

As shown in Fig. 3, both estimators correctly capture the decrease in hit ratio as μF\mu_{F} increases. However, for small μF\mu_{F}, the event that the interarrival time is not exponentially distributed (i.e., Wi​jE2E>Wi​jsampleW^{\text{E2E}}_{ij}>W^{\text{sample}}_{ij}) occurs more frequently, which makes the empirical mean interarrival time μ^F>μF\hat{\mu}_{F}>\mu_{F}. In contrast, for large μF\mu_{F}, the finite measurement horizon censors conversations with long interarrival times, which can make μ^F<μF\hat{\mu}_{F}<\mu_{F}. These effects explain the relative ordering of the prior and posterior estimates across different μF\mu_{F} regimes. Nevertheless, Fig. 4 shows that the absolute error remains below 0.020.02 throughout the experiment, while the relative error remains below 16%16\%. When the target and empirical interarrival means are close, i.e., 120≤μF≤165120\leq\mu_{F}\leq 165 s, the relative errors of both estimators are below 10%10\%.

In Experiment 2, to reduce the error caused by the mismatch between the target and realized interarrival distributions, we fix μF=135\mu_{F}=135 s, for which μ^F\hat{\mu}_{F} is closest to the target in Experiment 1. We vary the conversation arrival rate from 0.50.5 to 2.02.0. As shown in Fig. 5, both estimators correctly capture the decrease in empirical hit ratio as λ0\lambda_{0} increases. Moreover, the estimates are more accurate in this experiment. To be specific, we note in Fig. 6 that both estimators achieve absolute errors below 0.0150.015 and relative errors below 7%7\%.
